en: The Treasury of Dohās of Saraha-pāda. Homage to Śrī Vajrasattva!
Having paid constant and respectful homage to the Gurus, the Lords of the World, [I shall compose this].
The *Sahajāmnāyapañjikā* commentary on the *Dohākoṣa* is being written by Sarojapāda and Vajrapāda, following the traditional scriptures.
Nothing new has been set forth here; it was all spoken by the Blessed One in the past.
Those who rely on the six philosophical systems do not know the reality;
relying on arguments concerning birth and the like, they are useless [pretenders] to the status of Brahmins and so forth.
Having fallen away from liberation, despised by those whose souls seek liberation, they wander through the six states of existence.
Those who stand outside the two means of valid cognition— direct perception and inference—
and who, due to their lack of the authentic path, associate with evil friends; therefore,
the veneration of the Guru is always performed by the virtuous.
Through satisfaction with him, liberation shall come both in this world and in the next;
he respectfully bestows the true essence of everything as taught by the Tathāgata.
Herein, first, the six philosophical systems (ṣaḍdarśana) are set forth.

The author of the work speaks of these— the Brahmins, Īśvaras, Arhats, Buddhists, Lokāyatas, and Sāṃkhyas— in a sequence that deviates from their usual order, beginning with "vamhaṇehim" and ending with "ṇa jāṇia tullemi. (72)
In that regard, it is said for the purpose of refuting the Brahmins: "The Brahmins do not know the distinction. This means that the Brahmins do not know the difference or the specific subdivisions.
Therefore, he explains how there is a distinction for that which distinguishes:
first, there is a distinction of genus (*jāti-bheda*).
This is because their statement is that among the four castes, the Brāhmaṇa caste is the highest.
That is refuted by means of valid cognition, scripture, and reasoning.
Now, if one were a Brahmin by birth, [it would contradict] the statement: "The Brāhmaṇa was the mouth."
Then, at that time, it is said regarding the Brahmin: "This very one must be [the case].
How so?
Because here, there is the possibility of an origin other than the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa).

Therefore, because of prior existence, if there were not one [prior state], there could be no object considered as many. Even their statement that "that which was their face" is merely false speech, like the talk of a rogue.
Alternatively, one does not become a Brāhmaṇa by means of refinement (*saṃskāra*); such is the case.
"How could it not be so? he said.
"Even for one of the lowest caste (antyaja), a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) is performed;
how then could he not be a Brāhmaṇa?"
Therefore, birth is not established.
How then can the Veda be self-existent (*svayambhū*) in the absence of birth? He says:
"It is indeed produced from these very [elements] and from those four Vedas."
The four Vedas— the Ṛg, Sāman, Yajus, and Atharvan— were thus recited by those who knew the distinctions of caste;
and this is not inconsistent with respect to the lowest castes (antyajas).
And there is the case of the recitation-section (pāṭhādhikaraṇa),
because comprehension arises from both [the word and its meaning].
Now, if comprehension were to arise from the word alone—
Then it becomes common to all as well;
just as in grammar, the word "Vedānta" is established,
that very word alone is characterized by its transcendence of worldly usage.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as an ultimate reality;
nor is that which has the nature of sound eternal, even if it be self-existent.
How, then, can it be said to be eternal?
Just as the existence of the world does not exist because of its impermanence,
so too that authority which has dissolved within the Vedas does not exist.
There is a contradiction because of the absence of an agent (*kāraka*).
[Objection: If there is no village, how can there be a boundary?

[Response: How then is there no agent? It is said that it is because it is established by itself; moreover, that which has the nature of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) exists even in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the destruction of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Because it is dependently originated;
because there is no existence of the subsequent [effect] prior to [the cause]; because it appears like an illusion;
and because it is merely a conjunction.
Because it arises through delusion;
thus, not knowing that the entire cycle of existence is merely delusion, they wander through the six realms of rebirth.
Through the cessation of that [delusion], everything becomes perfectly secure.
By this also, it is shown that the Veda is not merely an action;
for when there is an absence of a cause, there is a metaphorical designation of an effect—
it is simply false, as explained in detail.
Therefore, when there is no authoritative means of knowledge, everything is performed; and that is expressed by the words "I am he" and so forth, up to "offering the oblation into the fire.
But what is the use of that *agnihotra*?
"By the *agnihotra* devoid of purpose"—
that is, by the *agnihotra* lacking a specific objective,
there is no offering (*homa*) of clarified butter and so forth.

And how is it that for those who do not know the ultimate truth, the fruit does not arise? In that case, even for an outcaste, such [a result] would occur purely by itself, as it is said: "The eye is burned by the bitter smoke."
Excessively pungent smoke causes a burning sensation in the eyes;
thus, there will be affliction by disease. How then [should one proceed]?
He states their essential nature:
"The Supreme Brahman.
And they describe that in various ways.
“Brahma-knowledge,” and so forth.
In that regard, “the supreme Brahman”:
through the oblation of the words of the sacrificer, they attain the status of the *brahman* priest.
And that [act] has as its fruit the enjoyment desired by those who wish for heaven; yet,
by means of that slaughter of the white goat, they experience the suffering of hell and other such realms.
And because they do not understand the intentional language (*sandhābhāṣa*), it is said,
"Brahman is [like] the killing of a Brahmin," and so forth;
for there is the statement that "everything is Brahman."
Thus it is said, "the knowledge of Brahman.
That too is not established.
Why? Because it is uncertain whether or not they possess the vision of the Yoga practice according to the Atharvaveda, the fourth Veda.

Even the mere recitation of the three Vedas is not established [for them]. Therefore, their speech is entirely false and uninterrupted by truth. Furthermore, nothing stated therein exists, including the knowledge of Brahman.
In that case, the authority of the three Vedas does not exist because they are thus negated;
nor does it exist for the fourth, the Atharva Veda,
because of mutual contradictions.
Therefore, how can the knowledge of Brahman be established through the scriptures? It remains unestablished. Or, if it were to become an experience...
Then that statement is utterly false.
Why? Because [it claims] that "everything is empty."
There is no apprehension of an object; how, then, could there be cognition of it?
Furthermore, since experience is apprehended as having a form, that very [experience] is what is intended by "cognition."
"Because of the non-apprehension of all things.
And a thing (*vastu*) is that which is imagined by the world, having ignorance as its nature;
it is not, however, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
And in our system, the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is obtained from the mouth of a true guru.
Thus, there are again four divisions of the Brāhmaṇa:
the student (brahmacārī), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), the householder (gārhapatya), and the ascetic (yati).
That too is inconsistent.
Why? Because in childhood there is no certainty regarding states such as protection or consumption.
Likewise, the state of celibacy (brahmacāritva) is undertaken by all philosophical systems through a firm vow for as long as life lasts;
they have no certainty that one might again resort to the household life through marriage and so forth.
And even in that case, there is no certainty;
they resort to the state of being forest-dwellers through such causes as meditation, mantra-recitation, and so forth. And even therein, if one desires the status of a *yati*, there is no certainty.
Because of wearing all the sacred threads and so forth, and because of consuming [the same food], there is no difference between a Brāhmaṇa and a Caṇḍāla;
by implication, he is indeed a Caṇḍāla.
This is true, for what reason? Because a Brāhmaṇa woman brings about degradation through a thief, a Caṇḍāla, or the like.
Then the Brahmin reflects upon the Veda,
thinking that by means of that [rite], purification might be achieved for that Brāhmaṇī through the creation of a womb of clarified butter (ghṛtayoni).
Therefore, all of this is indeed merely the work of a Caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, there are three further divisions even of the ascetic (yati): the single-staffed (daṇḍin) and so forth.
One becomes a *haṃsa* through the practice of the *uṣa* [vow], being without the attire of a householder, whether as a single-staffed or a triple-staffed ascetic.
Thus,
he assumes the appearance of a Blessed One as either a single-staffed or a triple-staffed ascetic;
he dwells in such a guise.
Furthermore, he causes this very vow to be abandoned;
he takes recourse in another.
This is precisely what it says: "Without [it], one becomes a swan in the upward breath."
As long as one does not assume the guise of a Paramahaṃsa, knowledge is not attained because of the necessity of total renunciation;
yet even that [guise] does not come about, for what reason? Because one is seized by the grasp of the latent impressions of ignorance (avidyāvāsanā).
This is directly perceived:

at the time of abandoning the *gārhapatya* fire, whatever wealth or property has been acquired, he gives all of that to his sons, grandsons, and so forth, rather than making it common to all living beings. He does not merely perform the ritual of descending from his lineage, thinking, "Because my family will not perish. Therefore—
O you foolish embodied beings, who always speak of evil deeds, you are ruined;
deluded by your past karma, you do not know the true reality at all.
Thus, being ruined yourselves, you ruin others as well.
He says this very thing in the verse beginning with *micchehiṃ*, etc.
(76): *micchehiṃ jaga vāhia bhūlleṃ* means that by false speech, the entire world—the foolish people—has been led onto evil paths. And this—

"Without knowing that dharma and adharma are equal"—here, "dharmas" refers to all entities consisting of the classes of sentient beings and so forth, as well as the objects of the senses; "adharmas" refers to others, devoid of those [objects], characterized by the body and so on. The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that they do not know the distinguished path, which is non-dual and equal with respect to both of these.
The detailed explanation of this has been set forth elsewhere in brief;
it is not, however, equal to merit, demerit, and so forth.
Now, that which depends upon Īśvara is being described.
"Airī" and so forth refers to the instruction regarding the south. Here,
"airiehiṃ uddūlia cchārehiṃ" means that one has smeared oneself with ash, [addressed as] "ayirī."
Thus, their limbs are smeared with external ashes because they have attained certainty regarding the Blessed One's teachings. Furthermore:
"They carry a mass of matted hair on their heads. They bear upon their heads a mass of matted locks formed from various kinds of hair. Moreover:
"He sits in the house like a lamp in a lattice" means that he remains in his own place having lit a lamp through the hypocrisy of the world.
"He rings the bell while sitting in a corner."
Taking recourse in the northeast corner, he rings the bell.
Again, in this very place:
"Having fixed his eyes, he binds his seat."
And this is the fundamental characteristic of hypocrisy (*kuhanā*):
it is performed by means of the opening and closing of the eyes;
having assumed a posture such as the full-lotus position (*paryaṅka*), and subsequently—(77)
"O dull-witted people, listen with your ears!
Having seen these aforementioned characteristics of the Arhat, those of dull intellect—who do not know what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—whisper it into their ears.
They deliberate among themselves: "This is the distinguished path; I am devoted to it, so listen, O people!"
"Also in other guises, such as a widow or a shaven-headed woman.
Here, "widow" (*raṇḍī*) refers to one who is without a husband;
"shaven-headed" (*muṇḍī*) refers to one who observes a month-long fast.
Others, however, are vow-observers (*vratini*) who do not assume possession (*anaveśadhāriṇī*).
By them, [the disciple] is led along his path.
Thus, to answer the question "What kind of teacher does he have?", he says:
Then it is seen exclusively; thus,
the reflection is perceived.

"What is that? It is 'for the sake of a teacher's fee' (gurūdakṣiṇā-uddeśena). Merely by designating it as a teacher's fee for their own sake, they cause sentient beings to fall into the afflictions."
And for those who do not know it themselves,
he says this very thing:
if one thinks that everything is God, it is not so.
How is it not so? He says: by means of valid cognition, scripture, and reasoning.
Therefore, it is stated here in brief: for in this context, there is no such thing as "name" that corresponds to any real entity whatsoever.
How is that so? Because all elements such as earth, as well as the atoms of the aggregate and the atoms of the form-body, are not perceived through a division into six parts;
at that time, the entity is no longer an entity.
Furthermore, how can God be accepted [as the cause], given that he is unestablished?
In the absence of the pervader, there is no perception of the pervaded.
Alternatively, if it is argued that they speak of "agency," then it is said in response: how is it that an eternal entity does not produce an effect either successively or simultaneously? (78)
Therefore, there is no external object for it, nor any internal one imagined by it. This very point he states:
"If it were capable [of acting], why would it depend on place, time, and so forth?"
Therefore, it could not exist simultaneously.
What would it create?
It would depend upon another entity.
It is neither eternal nor is it a power;
moreover, no entity is eternal. Why?
Furthermore, existence is momentary in all respects; moreover, it is not admitted [to exist] apart from the object and the subject. Why?
Because visible forms and so forth are perceived by means of the two eyes.
Because it is mere delusion:

even through investigation, since things such as pots and cloths are not perceived, how could atoms and the like—possessing the aforementioned characteristics—become objects [of cognition] due to their prior non-existence?
Just as the characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is not that atoms are external to the mass.
Furthermore, even the manifestation of appearances such as blue, yellow, and so forth does not occur.
Because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its existence as a self-nature (*ātman*) is non-existent.
How then could there be an engagement in visual consciousness and the other [sensory cognitions] through the relationship of grasped object and grasping subject?

Foolish people imagine that this is merely an error, thinking "this is white," "this is yellow," and so forth. Furthermore, it is said: even though it is not yellow and has not been repeatedly practiced, it goes back to its original state; how then could its cognition not be a continuous flow?
In that case, how is it not forgotten?
Furthermore, who—being devoid of action—could produce the extreme measurement of the great ocean arising from the mountains of Vaiṣamyashaila, as well as the dimensions of the most subtle atoms?
If you argue that he does so by virtue of his possession of power, [we reply:]...
He becomes like one who is insane;
for at the time of destruction, how could he avoid exhausting himself?
Or rather, it is simply rendered powerless.
Furthermore, the attraction of weapons and other objects by magnets and the like is denied;
that [attraction] is moreover denied in the context of the arrival of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is because the body is not a locus for the application of mindfulness (*anusmṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth; rather, through investigation, the body is seen as a contemptible cage and devoid of substantial reality (*avastu*). Thus it is said: (79)
One should sever the flesh from the skeletal frame with the sword of wisdom;
having separated the bones as well, look at the marrow within. Having investigated for oneself, ask: "What essence is there here?"
"This body, a mere vessel of strife, is always filled with saliva, urine, feces, vapors, blood, sweat, intestines, marrow, and fat; it constantly exudes impurity through its wound-like openings.
Therefore, there is no abiding place for consciousness; it is merely a product of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)."
And that [self] arises through the power of ignorance;
by means of it, all defects come into being.
Thus it has been said: "When there is a self, there is the notion of 'other'; from the division of self and other, there arise attachment and aversion."
All faults arise when these two are conjoined;
therefore, the characteristic of dependent origination is well-established.
Alternatively, if one relies upon some deity or a physical body, that [reliance] does not [lead to liberation].
Why? If God does not exist, what else could she accomplish apart from him?
Because of the statement that she is "composed of him" (tanmaya), therefore it is not so.
Now, if it is argued that simultaneous experience is being established, that too is not possible;
for the existence of inference has not yet been proven.
If, on the other hand, one performs an incursion such as shaking or trembling, then people would perceive it as a real manifestation of the *kuhika* spirit;
however, because [the spirit] is unobservable, that too does not occur for one who experiences it within themselves. This very point he states:
Tell me, what indeed can be said regarding its being known by each individual for themselves? For those who claim that it is an entity to be personally realized, its nature is described as follows:
it is urged that it is impossible to say of it, "This is it."

The virtuous, however, always act with unerring consistency in order to produce certainty in others regarding their own certainty. That which is the object of cognition for the cognizer does not exist in the absence of the object of cognition; without the object of cognition, there is no cognizer.
"Since the object of cognition and the cognizer are thus non-existent, why is [dependent origination] not accepted?
Therefore, that which depends upon a Lord (Īśvara) has been refuted as being merely dependent origination.
Now, the position of the Kṣapaṇakas is addressed.
In this regard, the passage beginning with *dīhaṇakkhajai* and ending with *tāva para kevala sāhai* means:
"Thus, by means of a long night, a soiled appearance,
and a disguise, all embodied beings in every world who rely upon the Arhants have been devoured through deceit and hypocrisy."

Wearing soiled garments and themselves ignorant of the ultimate reality, they again inflict suffering upon their own bodies. Regarding them, he says: "O naked one, you have achieved nothing by plucking out your hair. By the act of plucking out one's hair while naked, no higher purpose whatsoever is attained.
"What would happen if it were spoken thus? [The answer is:
"Know that even by the Kṣapaṇakas, the mockery of the path is not of such a kind. That is to say, the mockery of the path practiced by the Kṣapaṇakas is not like this.
Why?
Because of the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal; and because those who do not know that path resort to them [the false teachers], saying:
"By means of the self, one attains liberation."

Having directed one’s own self toward evil deeds and wrong paths with the aim of liberation, that liberation is not achieved; for it will be stated later: "If liberation were indeed nakedness... and so forth.

If liberation belongs to those who are submerged [in the mud], then—listen to the jackal!—why does liberation not belong to dogs, jackals, and the like? Or else: (81) "If there is accomplishment through the plucking out of hair..."
If there were accomplishment through the plucking out of body hair, then why would there not be liberation from the hips of young women?
For it is the constant practice of young women to pluck their hair;
[if that led to success], why would they not be freed from their hips? Or else—

"By grasping the peacock feather, liberation was seen"—if liberation were seen by the *kṣapaṇaka* through the grasping of a peacock feather, then [what of this]: "therefore, seize the horses"? In that case, would there not be hidden wings on elephants and horses?
Liberation occurs through the garland of peacock-feather ornaments;
that is to say, it does not occur otherwise. Furthermore:
"Know that [liberation] occurs in the gathering of alms for food."

"If knowledge arises through food obtained by gleaning, then [I shall do so]," and so forth, as before—Saraha says: "The liberation of the *kṣapaṇakas* does not appear as anything at all to me. Saroruha-vajrapāda stated that the liberation of the *kṣapaṇakas* does not appear to him in the slightest degree.

When their established doctrine is that the characteristic of the group of living beings (*jīvanikāya*) and so forth is impermanence, yet they further maintain the statement that "the life-force (*jīva*) belongs to the lords of the forest," then one asks: why does this not hold? He says: when there is the destruction of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, then [that entity] is indeed impermanent. Thus, there is one group of living beings, while the second consists of the lords of the forest, such as grasses, woods, and groves. (82)
The third consists of the four elements beginning with earth; likewise, there are the six classes of living beings. All of this does not exist.
Why?
Because all elements are insentient;
where, then, can life be found within them?
It means that it is not obtained.
Now, as for the life-force (*jīva*) being dependent on the person (*puruṣa*):
that has already been refuted previously in the refutation of the Lord (*īśvara*).
What would follow from what has been said?
Everything would be of an impermanent nature.
How, then, is there the state of being dependently originated?
And dependent origination is of the nature of delusion,
because the world lacks stability;
having abandoned this world, it proceeds to the heavens and other realms.

Even those who have attained awakening perform the welfare of sentient beings in this life, and then, through the transformation of the aggregates, go to another world to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings; subsequently, by relinquishing that [state], they again take up the aggregates and so forth.
This occurs at all times, like a whirling firebrand.
[This is] due to previous causes and vows;
however, the distinction is that... like an illusion, it is neither true nor false.
Furthermore, it is established that while the world has a form of appearance, its true nature is eternal.
It is not like that of the Arhats;
however, for them, there is no liberation in the form of permanence.
Why? Because their teaching holds that liberation is like a parasol over the three realms.
And that [world-system] measures eighty-six thousand yojanas;
yet this very thing is not established. For since there is the destruction of the triple world, where would the parasol remain?
Therefore, liberation does not have the nature of permanence; it must be impermanent. This is the summary; it should be understood in detail elsewhere.
Now, that which pertains to the *śramaṇas* is stated:
therein, from "cellu" and so forth up to "sāhiu paryantam," [it means] "the elder monks (*bhikṣus*) who are senior (*sthaviras*) by their instruction."
"I pay homage to the one who has gone forth in the guise of a lay follower. (83) A *cella* possesses ten precepts; a *bhikṣu* possesses ten million precepts.
An elder is one who has attained ten years [of seniority].
All of them take up the renunciant life merely for the sake of the outward appearance of wearing saffron robes;
therefore, they do not practice the conduct of teaching, begging for alms, morality, or patience.
They do not know reality as it truly is;
under the guise of deceit and hypocrisy, they harass sentient beings.

As the Blessed One said: "In the future time, in the final age, when I have passed into parinirvāṇa and during the era of the five corruptions, those monks who shall exist within my teaching will all be devoted to deceit and hypocrisy."
They will come into being.
Likewise, when the building of houses occurs, those devoted to agriculture, trade, and so forth will commit all manner of sinful deeds.
Mockers of the Teaching—those who were formerly of Māra’s host—all of them will descend upon the earth in the guise of śramaṇas.

In that regard, there is the detailed passage beginning with, "The elders of the Saṃgha in the midst will seize the property for the use of the Saṃgha," and so forth. How is it that they [do not] attain awakening?
For those who rely on the Śrāvakayāna, there is destruction according to the characteristics already described.
Upon its dissolution, they go again to hell.
Furthermore, by the mere preservation of the training, there is only the enjoyment of heaven according to the characteristics described in the Vinaya;
the supreme enlightenment, however, does not arise—why? Because when the Elder Āryānanda passed into parinirvāṇa, he did not transmit it to anyone.
That would be an instruction on the enlightenment of the śrāvakas.
Alternatively, if they resort to the Mahāyāna,
even there no certainty arises.
Why? Because he previously belonged to the category of those who destroy [the Dharma].
Even if he were well-established, that too would be uncertain; this very point is stated:
"Someone who is a speaker of the Sūtras and a teacher of the Vākya... etc.
In some cases, a monk gives an exposition on reality;
because he has not heard it before, he again goes to the hells and other realms, and this is due to greed for wealth and the like.

(84) "Who thinks? Who dries up what is seen?"—in some cases, all phenomena are indeed made by the mind; they say this while reflecting upon the letters of the scriptures and their treatises, and thus he performs the practice, thinking, "I shall see."
Because he does not understand the recitation, he will go to a state of woe;
even by such thoughts, he causes the withering of his mind.
Those diseases arose;
they will depart by means of the great medicines found there.
And by means of that delusion, one goes to the states of woe.
Therefore, what is called "delusion" is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Liberation comes from abandoning delusion. Thus...
"Thus, in the ultimate sense, you have been shown to be one.
By that ascetic and others, through reasoning, it has been established that the disciples and others are ultimately one;
their engagement [in practice] is solely for the sake of livelihood through the performance of vows and so forth.
Regarding that, he states the collective meaning:

"Whosoever is satisfied by whatever [view], for him the Blessed One has shown the mere path, such as the Śrāvaka-yāna and so forth, within those vehicles. This means that whichever view by which one becomes contented—for him, the Blessed One has demonstrated only the path, such as the Śrāvaka-yāna and others, within those respective vehicles.
Having entered, they attain liberation;
that is to say, it does not consist of the relationship between the signified and the signifier.
That [state] is brought about...
"It is so difficult to attain.
Thus, the group consisting of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others, being devoid of the true reality (*tattva*), said:
"What is the island? What is the refuge? and so forth.
What is the use of showing [the deity], and what is the use of prostration? What indeed should be done by means of the service of the mantra?
Alternatively, what is the use of a lamp, what is the use of an offering of food? Due to the absence of knowledge, nothing at all is accomplished. Likewise:
(85) "What is the use of a holy ford, a penance grove, or birth there?"—what indeed would a holy ford be [in that case], and so forth?

But what is gained by going to a penance grove? Is liberation obtained merely by water? By this statement, it is asked: is liberation obtained through resorting to sacred fords (*tīrtha*), purified by bathing in their waters?
It means "is not obtained.

"Abandon, O friends, these false bonds! means that persons seeking what is to be relinquished should cast off false attachments such as those toward spiritual teachers (tīrtha) and the like, which have been described by the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
By which you will go to hell and other realms;
for the sake of the world, [you teach] those views and so forth:
"There is no gift, there is no oblation, there are no ascetics, and there are no brahmins."
"There is no future world; as long as one lives, let one live happily, for one is beyond the reach of death.
Once the body has been reduced to ashes, how can there be a return? This is because of their nihilistic view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Alternatively, the Sāṃkhyas say:

"The Sāṃkhyas maintain that *pradhāna* is eternal and the cause of the world," and so forth; [if it is asked] what is accomplished by that [eternity], [the answer is] "it does not bring about welfare. If this is objected:
"Therefore, abandon that which you remain stuck in," and so forth.
Indicating a distinguished practice by means of the collective sense [of these words], he says:
"Cultivate resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) toward the true paths."
By doing which you will accomplish your own purpose;
by abandoning the improper path and relinquishing it, you will not remain in a state of sluggishness,
but will proceed without hindrance along the true path.
"It is indeed the innate itself, nothing else. Thus: "In the thorough knowledge of that, there is no other whatsoever.
In the thorough knowledge of that innate [nature], there is no other liberation whatsoever.
All these, O Gaṇeśa, are likewise [transient].

Whatever various collections of liberation have been conceptualized separately by all others, all that is indeed the innate (*sahaja*) and nothing else. Yet, not knowing that innate state, they wander in saṃsāra like a waterwheel.
And that [innate state] is attained by one who has taken refuge in a true guru.
In that regard, within the innate (*sahaja*), neither the signified (*vācya*) nor the signifier (*vācaka*) is found.
(86) Due to the relationship between the signified and the signifier, the innate does not exist in the three [realms].
It was established by the Blessed One in certain instances through the application of the basis for teaching.
And while the book is being observed for the sake of sentient beings, it is not perceived as such;
whatever object one sees, such as the conceptualization of form and so forth as being illusory, that very object would not be seen as non-illusory through the lineage of the gurus. Therefore:
"Thus it is recited," and so forth.
Whatever there may be, such as reading, private study (*svādhyāya*), and the like—consisting of the natural flow of scriptures, purāṇas, and so on—they pass away.
He states that this applies not only to the supramundane but also to the mundane:
It is explained in the *Satthapurāṇa* as follows:
"Whatever exposition of the scriptures, Purāṇas, and so forth is made, all of that pertains only to the Sahaja and nothing else. Thus it says:
"He does not possess true vision who does not perceive that [Sahaja]."
Thus, according to the sequence described as being innate (*sahaja*), as long as it is not perceived by persons, liberation is not seen by them—
that [perception] which effects the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) in that very instant.
To the question "How is it to be seen?", he says:
"Ekkeṃ vara," and so forth.
By this, which consists solely of the excellent and most eminent Guru’s instruction, [the goal] is indicated.
Thus, he speaks for the sake of clarity:
"If what the guru has spoken enters the heart"— that is, when the path taught by the guru becomes established within the heart— then:
(87) "Only she is seen standing right here."

Just as when a person obtains a *cintāmaṇi* jewel somewhere, they certainly perform acts such as giving for its sake; so too here, once the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*) has been attained, it makes all sentient beings consist of that very nature, like a *cintāmaṇi*, and causes one to relinquish all possessions, wealth, and the like.
Out of ignorance of such a path,
the author Saraha expresses lamentation with the words "The world is carried away" (*jaga vāhia āleṃ*), and so forth.
"The entire world has been carried away by the indolence of the heterodox practitioners and others;
thus, its own nature has not been perceived by the foolish.
By those of such a foolish nature, this innate state, which is one's own true essence, has not been perceived.
They have not propitiated true gurus;
therefore, they experience the suffering of the six realms of existence and so forth. This applies not only to the heretic, but also regarding [the failure to propitiate gurus] among the śramaṇas.

"Even one devoid of meditation remains in the state of renunciation"—this means that when a śramaṇa, though lacking right knowledge, has performed the characteristics of renunciation such as the observance of discipline (vinaya) and so forth, there is no fruit for him.
Why? It is said: "Living at home, he would have been better off."
When one does not undertake the stage of life beginning with the construction of a house, there is a violation of the vow; by that, there is a violation of all [rules] such as the conduct (*caryā*).
It is not the case that by the violation of one single promise there is a violation of all, just as when one person consumes poison, it does not affect all living beings.
Destruction occurs;
and thus, when one person dies, there arises for all the fear of death from poison, even if [the poison] has not been consumed.
Then, whatever it may be... (88)
Having thoroughly examined it, one consumes all of that;
or else, one practices the reality of poison (*viṣatattva*).
And because of that, from the very beginning, there is firm certainty; otherwise, a failure occurs.

Thus, whatever observances and practices are undertaken, all of them are for the sake of firm resolve. And regarding that: "If one does not abandon the attachment to the enjoyment of sense objects"—that is, if one does not relinquish the delight in firmly indulging in the objects of the senses.
Then the author [asks]:
"What is gained by the thorough knowledge [of others]? To this he replies: "What is said by that other thorough knowledge? Because of the non-abandonment of momentary pleasure."
By means of which they experience suffering;
yet, even when there is full comprehension (*parijñāna*), they are not liberated through the pursuit of sense objects, such as the five desires and so forth.
Then, what is the point of speaking of other forms of "dry" comprehension? That is to say, why are they not liberated when such [dry] comprehension is expressed?
If it is directly perceptible, then what is accomplished by meditation? If it is beyond perception, then do not consider it as darkness.
If it is directly perceptible, then what is accomplished by meditation?
When this is imperceptible and not seen in the midst of darkness, what is seen?
What would be implied by this?
Why are all the vows, such as renunciation and the like, being performed?
And because the fruit of the next world is not seen in the midst of darkness, it is [known] through the reason of inference. What is that direct perception? He says: "Saraheṃ," and so forth.
A cry was drawn out;
it was not kept secret by me among all people, but was uttered as a great roar with extreme clarity.
What was that?
"Innate nature is neither existence nor non-existence.
Here, "existence" refers to that object which [is perceived] through the light of the eyes and other senses, as well as through the mental construction of the mind. Why is that so?
Since the entire world of phenomena has been produced by the nature of the innate (*sahaja*), one is liberated through the conceptualization of it as being thus.
And so it has been said: (89) "Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added."
"The real must be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated.
How does he state the reasoning for this?
"This is that which has arisen through the happiness of the two-footed."
And those desiring happiness are born from the union of mother and father; since this is personally experienced by each individual, it is not non-existent. Why?
And because it is inexpressible due to being identical with that [reality], the sense is that this very state is the bliss that ends with death. Therefore:
"He suffers, dies, accumulates [karma], or is bound."
"By this, supreme great bliss is accomplished. Thus it is said.
By that very bliss through which they die, by that same they are born; and having been born, they are bound within that very state.
And this is according to the conception of worldly happiness.
The meaning is that by correctly understanding and grasping the instruction from that very guru, one accomplishes supreme great bliss (*paramamahāsukha*).
Thus, the passage beginning with "Saraha" and so forth is easy to understand.
He provides a specific explanation of this:
"What is to be done with meditation that is devoid of dhyāna?
What can be described there, since it is soundless?
Thus [it is said]. Here, first of all, primordial knowledge (jñāna) is devoid of the characteristics of the signified and the signifier, and so forth.
Therefore, why is this innate knowledge treated as something imagined? Because it is devoid of a cause,
there is no established result.
Therefore, what explanation can be given for that which is inexpressible?
As it has been said: "In this way, everything is false as long as it is conceptualized. (90) Thus far.
"That is the truth; that is suchness, the reality which is not conceptualized. To the question "What is that?", he further says:
"Its nature is considered to be transparent, formless, and stainless."
"And it is not possible for that [nature] to be known in any way among those who are unawakened;
even a Buddha does not know it in the same manner as this other person [the ordinary being].
For he alone knows that very [nature] by depending upon it. Thus [it is said].
Therefore, since reality is not characterized by the functioning of ignorance, he asks: "What is this ignorance? and says:
"O, the entire world has been carried away by delusion; its own nature has not been realized by anyone. Thus it is said.
The entire world is carried away by the seal of existence (*bhavamudrā*). Marked with the seal of existence, those whose hearts are stainless are deceivers of sentient beings;
by her, the world is enslaved, and whatever she desires—such as the taking of life—they are made to perform all that through desire and greed.
And she acted like a madwoman.
Therefore, one's own true nature, which is the perfect reality, has not been realized by anyone.
Furthermore, the world has been deluded by the greed for material wealth through the teachings on mantras, tantras, and so forth. To that [delusion], he says:

"Neither mantra, nor tantra, nor dhyāna, nor dhāraṇā"— by this [statement], the author has declared out of compassion that liberation is not attained by being devoid of mantra and tantra. "By all those [means], O fool, only the cause of delusion [is produced]."
Thus, O fool, in all states of existence, delusion (*vibhrama*) is the cause of worldly power and the cause of prosperity;
because of that error, one experiences suffering. Therefore:
"Do not soil the stainless mind with meditation" means: do not, for the time being, smear the pure mind with ignorance.
How is that said to be stainless?
The designation "mind" is twofold: mundane and supramundane.
That which is mundane has the characteristic of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and was previously refuted.
That which is supramundane, stainless, characterized as the Dharmakāya, or the innate nature (sahajasvarūpa); for this very reason it is said:
"While remaining in bliss, do not quarrel with yourself.
By this, the entire triple world is established as being of the nature of non-conceptual bliss.
Then do not cause others to suffer through separation from the self;
then make this [world] consist of happiness. What does he say regarding that?
"khāante" and so forth, up to "u bhaaloaha paryantam."
And by this, the practice with conceptual elaboration (*saprapañcacaryā*) is also indicated, as it was performed by Indrabhūti:
[it involves] eating and drinking,
but not the play of sexual union in the enjoyment of the five objects of desire.
Furthermore, having taken [the offering] with a vessel of lotus petals and so forth, he will present the bali offering;
he will abide in the form of the deities of the great maṇḍala.
By this, the accomplishment of gnosis and the accomplishment of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) shall arise for fortunate beings.
And by means of those [powers], he places his foot upon the heads of the many fearsome beings of the world, including the non-Buddhist heretics and others;
thus he disciplines them.

Regarding this, he states what the objective is of that Mahāmudrā which is to be accomplished: (92) "When the mind and breath no longer wander, and neither the sun nor the moon enters [the central channel], then, O Citta, take rest; tell me, by whom has the path been traversed? Thus it is said.

Wherever, by the instruction of the Guru, one's own nature is established through self-awareness within all living beings— even in those who do not desire it— there one should bring about the rest of the mind, wherein greatness will be attained; in that place, there is no movement of either the mind or the vital breath.
In that very state, there is neither the entry nor the exit of the sun and the moon;
yet it is not a mere mental construction, for all [faculties] become completely restrained.
Just as children, ignorant of the intentional language (saṃdhābhāṣya), imagine the restraint of the mind, breath, and so forth to be the basis, how can that be said to apply here?

"Nirodha" (cessation) is a term signifying negation. What is the use of that painful practice? As long as the body is driven by the vital airs (*vāyu*) and so forth, the body is either restrained or killed by the restraint of those airs.
Therefore, it should be understood through the instruction of a true guru.
The passage beginning with "Sara" and so forth is easy to understand.
However, the *bodhicitta* is of the nature of wind (*pavana*).

Then the mind becomes nectar, the very nature of bliss; thus, where neither the sun nor the moon—neither passion nor dispassion—is perceived as either imagined or innate, such is the state attained through this instruction.
From "Do one thing" (*ekku kurū*) up to "Ask the Guru clearly" (*phuḍa pucchahi gurū pāvā*), the meaning is easy to understand.
However, [this state] is pervaded by all instructions.
Therefore, one should act so that everything becomes identical with that; this is the intended meaning.
If at any time there should be doubt, then once again inquire in the presence of the Guru’s feet for the sake of greater clarity, so that you will become free from error.
Then he too will give that instruction, which he states as "Abandon the mind," and so forth.
"Where the mind dies and the breath goes to destruction"—
for it is established by this statement that not only those two, but something else as well, "this is that supreme great bliss which does not go anywhere."
And that which has been attained through the meditative absorption of supreme great bliss is also devoid [of inherent nature] without the correct instruction of the Guru.
Since there is an absence of both the signified and the signifier, how could even that reality be anything at all?
But it does not abide as "remaining";
it goes nowhere, nor has it gone anywhere.
The sense is that speech is not something that can be grasped by speech.
And so it has been said:
"Because it is beyond the range of the intellect, there is no introduction of discourse concerning the reality renowned from the Teacher, for such discourse cannot proceed through words.
Nevertheless, that [reality] gradually establishes its own footing within the hearts of those possessed of faith, who are purified by qualities such as compassion."
Right here it is said: "O slow-witted ones, do not practice self-awareness;
existence and non-existence are but bonds for a good rebirth.
(94) By means of the conceptualization of beginningless self-awareness, you will not attain bliss.
If you act with delay, you will go to ruin.

Therefore, O fool, whether it be an existence characterized as previously described, or even non-existence, or a "good rebirth" that is conceptually constructed—all of that cannot possibly be Buddhahood.
There is no difference between gold and an iron shackle; therefore [it is not Buddhahood].
"It must indeed be abandoned.
And so it has been said:
"Even regarding conceptual constructions concerning the ultimate reality, the wise man should not become attached."
For what difference is there in conceptual construction regarding whether an object is auspicious or even inauspicious?
There is no difference in the burning power of fire due to a difference in its substrate;
when touched, it burns indeed, whether ignited by sandalwood or otherwise.
To the question "What should be done by this?", he says:
"O wise ones, know your own mind, just as the ocean is known when it merges with the water. Thus.

You shall behold the mind as subtle, stainless, devoid of existence and non-existence, and consisting of luminosity. O you yogis, through subtle yoga— yoga being characterized by one-pointedness of mental fluctuations or characterized by the knower and the known— that [mind] becomes like water mixed with water,
provided that such yoga exists.
"O fool, what liberation do you seek through meditation that is like a mirage? What net of delusion do you grasp with your mind?
Thus, O deluded person, what liberation do you attain through false meditation, which appears like a mass of hair or other such illusions?
Therefore, that triad is difficult to overcome. Why?
Why grasp the entire web of illusion—the three worlds—within the embrace of one's own limbs? It is simply that it cannot be contained. However—(95) "Trust all the words of the excellent teacher."
Saraha says: "O brother, let it be recited. Thus, if there is indeed truth in the words of the Guru, then this has been spoken by me, Sarorūpapravara, through the *Dohā-kośa* and other works.

"If one is purified through the state of non-expectation"—thus, when conviction in the teacher's word has been established, whatever exertion toward all states of being occurs, that becomes pure. Why?
Because "at every step, at every step, vision is obstructed."
Just as when one looks with the eye, through gazing and by the cessation of blinking and opening, there occurs the cessation of the perception of mirages and such things as water from a distance;
in the very same way, here too, by means of investigation, everything becomes identical with that [reality]. It does not become so otherwise. What, then, is being investigated?
Accompanied by the manifestation of the guru’s oral instructions through the [spiritual] composition,
and provided that it is not like the web of conceptual meditations and so forth, then, by means of that very [instruction], one produces Buddhahood in dependence upon it.
And because it is like light due to the absence of darkness, or like sunlight due to the absence of shadow, a distinguished *nirmāṇakāya* arises herein.
But through the cessation of the mind, one comes to have the nature of the distinguished Dharmakāya; and that is "all-pervading"—this is the intended meaning. It is not, however, [merely] the mind.
Thinking that "nothing at all would exist," it produces that cognition; and because of its being dependently originated, it says this to those who do not understand it thus: (96)
"Eseṃ jai āāsa-vikālo | niamaṇa doseṇa na bujjhai bālo ||" (If this were the time for the cessation of all exertions, the fool would not understand it through the fault of his own mind.
The meaning is: if such a thing were the "vikāla" of exertions—not the time for their arising, but rather the time for the dissolution of all things.
At that time, due to the fault of being attached to their own mental conceptions, those of a childish nature—such as the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) and others—do not understand this.

This is what is meant: "Therefore, here, along with the Vedāntins, the Sāṃkhyas and the Kṣapaṇakas are considered to have their intellects deceived; though they have known the ultimate reality, their minds are firmly fixed on a view of a single self by means of a condensed synthesis."

Because the time for their discipline has not yet arrived, they have been neglected even by those of great compassion; further strengthening the very knots of saṃsāra, they are indeed objects of pity.
Since they are situated in calamity, they are not worthy of hatred for those endowed with compassion. As for those who follow the guide of the Sugata, they too [possess] the cognition of reality.

Those who are adept at discerning the worldly and the transcendental sides are not deceived by those whose intellects merely follow well-proclaimed doctrines; such is the detailed explanation. Therefore:
"The reality was not perceived due to the fault of pride.
Thus, the reality was not understood because of the faults of false knowledge and arrogance.
"By him, the entire vehicle is defiled; that is Datta. Thus, by their being defective, the entire vehicle and the path are defiled.
Like a Daitya-man... by this...
"Thus, the entire world is deluded by meditative absorption (jhāṇaṃ);
that is to say, all people—including those of other sects and the like—regard their own respective vehicles as the [only] vehicle.
"Therefore, no one perceives its own true nature."

Because it abides at all times as its own innate nature (*sahaja*), it has not been perceived by anyone in the world who is shrouded in ignorance; thus the author utters this lament. Again: (97) "The root of the mind was not perceived as *sahaja*—all three [worlds] are therein."
"In that [world] one lives, there one goes to dissolution, and there alone one remains; here [in this world], it is merely a flicker.
By this, he confirms the firmness of the instruction.
"Of the mind" (*cittaha*) refers to the singular instruction regarding *cintā* (reflection).
Thus, the root is not perceived—that which is not established in the word of the gurus is the second [aspect].
The innate nature (*sahaja*) is perceived by the perceiver as having the form of an intrinsic nature.
In this way, the triad of reality—consisting of the object of perception, the characteristic, and the perceiver—is false and unreal.
If it is grasped, then all things become of the nature of consciousness and mental factors;
by this, the existence of instruction would not be possible.
In that state, heroic men who are living, brave, and rare yogis are born.
Therefore, O son, one should dwell in such states.
In that state, all phenomena are dissolved; that is called the ultimate reality (paramārtha). He says this very thing:
"Victorious is the unique King of Bliss, devoid of causes, eternally arisen for the worlds."
And at the time of describing whom even the Omniscient One became impoverished of words—
it was thus that Mūlarāja contemplated the reality.
"By the instruction of the guru, this much is known"—
thus, whoever contemplates the reality that is devoid of a root,
[it is said]: "This reality has been realized by the jewels among men through the instruction of the guru."
"It is realized for one who travels by the path that is neither stable nor unstable, through the instruction of the Guru; it is perfected.
(98) Saraha says: "Know this, O noble one!
It is the destruction of the world of mental forms. Thus.
By this, the author states a clear meaning:
whatever cultivation of the nature of mind there may be, that would become a cause for fear of saṃsāra;
therefore, it was said.

The meaning is that through the instruction of the guru and firm conviction, that which is of the nature of the mind is perceived as reality; since saṃsāra consists of the mind, its destruction becomes possible.
Therefore, that is reality.
"One's own nature has not been told by another.

Thus, one's own nature—the very essence of the Self-born (Svayambhū)—has not been explained by others, such as the followers of other schools (tīrthikas). To whom, then, was it told? He says: "By the true gurus."
"It is seen through the instruction of the Guru, not by anyone else.
Thus, it was seen by me, Saraha, through the instruction of the True Guru and by taking refuge in the Sugata, and not by anyone else;
it was understood through the eye of the Guru’s instruction.
Regarding the statement "he is mute in this matter" intended for disparagement,
the author describes the quality of one who possesses such [a state]: "In the boat, he remains alone on the bank."
There is no single location for that fault by which one might consume dharma and adharma as clarified butter;
rather, through the instruction of the Guru, dharma and adharma— possessing the characteristics previously described— are to be purified.
One partakes of that which has been purified. Regarding its specific ritual procedure, he says: (99) "Having purified all through self-restraint (*niyama*)."
In this way, all phenomena are mindless, arisen by their own nature, and not produced by anyone.

Just as grass, forests, shrubs, and so forth, arise by their own nature and undergo dissolution, so too here, bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth, arise by their own nature and pass away mindlessly; for they are not produced by anyone at all.
How, then, is it perceived?
[The thought] "These forms and so forth were created by me at their arising" is the speech of the ignorant, due to delusion.

Through the abandonment of that, at the very moment in which there is the purification of all phenomena, it becomes consumed due to being identical with that—“The qualities of the Guru enter the heart; by that [it is consumed]. Thus it is said.

The quality of the instruction given by the gurus has entered one’s own heart; for it is through the conviction that at times such as purification and eating, the entire body and so forth are offered therein.
They do not dispute the guru’s instruction, nor does it give anything away, because its nature is that of a seizer (*graha*); thus, the sense is that it does not know [anything else].
Thus: "In this way, Maṇi, Muṇi, and Saraha have grasped it."
Such is that which is characterized by the mind, the "mind-characterized.
Alternatively, in this way the venerable sage Saroruhavajrapāda has stated the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-rūpaka*):
it is the characteristic of the *dharmadhātu*, and not, like a rabbit's horn, something non-existent or without mind.
And so it has been said:
"That certain state which is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is incomprehensible to those like me;
it is not, however, like the conventional worldly view that conforms to the meaning of nihilism."
Its very non-existence is its existence for the sake of conventional usage;
for among phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, what could there be to exist or not exist? (100) When it is said, "You must not remember," one indeed remembers that which was prohibited.
"Just as from the word 'non-existent' one understands that which has something superior," and so forth in detail.
Alternatively, if they say that through practice, by way of opposing the mind shrouded by afflictions, a distinguished mind in the form of Buddhahood arises.
In that case, what would be achieved by this statement?
[The opponent might argue: "It is established for me that the ultimate reality (paramārtha) resides in all things. To this he replies: "That is not so; how so? He says:
"Thus,
not even one among the many types of tantras and the mantras taught therein has been examined by me as a single entity characterized by the nature of the manifested and the manifestor."
How could those [teachings] bring about anything more than the mere conversion of people; no distinguished fruit arises from them?
And so it has been said:
"By means of the yoga of the resolve for the bone [meditation], she is naturally pure from the very beginning."
For that suchness is established by its very nature and is not born of conceptual construction;
awakening has the characteristic of non-existence, and all phenomena consist of that. Therefore, one should aspire to that practice which is like a raft for one's own aggregates. Thus it is said.

Therefore: "One is bound by karma, but through liberation from karma, there is liberation of the mind. By means of that karma by which living beings are bound, through the resolute intention (*adhimokṣa*) of its abandonment, there occurs liberation of the mind.
And liberation consists in being free from the conceptualization of "self" and "mine"; for since the very notion of "mind" is a bond due to false cultivation, its cessation constitutes liberation.
Thus, regarding this thorough knowledge, he states the essential meaning [of liberation] as occurring simultaneously with the liberation of the mind:
"By the liberation of the mind, the supreme nirvāṇa is attained for those without faults.
This means "by the liberation of the mind."

The mind (*mana*) and liberation (*mokṣa*): the attainment of these two, which are mutually determined yet distinct from one another, is characterized by supreme *nirvāṇa*. As it is said: "The entire universe and both existence and *nirvāṇa* manifest within that single consciousness (*citta*).

When such *nirvāṇa* as described has been attained, and when the mind is thus bound [to its true nature], then from that consciousness all the seeds of ignorance, as well as those consisting of existence and *nirvāṇa*, manifest in an inconceivable manner.
That [state] does not exist as something remaining within cyclic existence (bhava);
therefore—“Bow down to that form of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), which grants the fruits of one’s desires.
This is an epithet of supreme nirvāṇa.
He, in the form of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel, performs prostration for him.
Why? For the reason that [the jewel] grants the fruit of one's desires.

And "desire" (*icchā*) is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), whose essence is the welfare of the world; he by whom the fruit of that longing is fulfilled effortlessly—he alone is his guru. Thus, he is like the *cintāmaṇi*. In this way—
"The mind is bound when it is bound; when it is liberated, there is no doubt.
When the mind is bound by conceptual constructions and the like, beings are bound;
furthermore, through the thorough knowledge of that [mind], they will attain liberation.
Thus, among those who are bound, liberated, both liberated and bound, liberation occurs through non-duality; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, due to lack of full understanding, those of a childish nature wander in saṃsāra, while the wise are liberated.
"By that very thing by which the dull-witted are bound, by that same thing the wise are swiftly liberated.

That is to say: by that very means—such as the enjoyment of deceptive desires and the like—by which the foolish world is bound, by that same means, when there is full understanding through the instruction of a guru, the learned are swiftly and quickly liberated from saṃsāra.
And so it has been said:
(102) "By that very same portion of poison by which all living beings die, one who knows the reality of the ritual should expel the poison with that very poison. Thus it is.
Furthermore:
"Bound, he runs; released, he stands motionless.

Just as a person, being bound by his own mental constructs, runs in the ten directions and wanders through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) of the six realms of rebirth, so too that very same person, when released from the right path, then [remains] in the self-liberated state, motionless.

The sense is that because he remains in his proper place, he is of the nature of the *dharmakāya*. "Look at this camel, friend; it seems to me it has been playing," [he says]. In this collective context, just as when a camel (*karabha*) is bound by a heavy load, it runs with speed, unable to bear [the weight].
Having been liberated from the flow of speech, remaining motionless and fixed in a single place for a moment, he thus directly experiences his own mind as being like a young elephant.
Such is my intuition, based on the characteristics described for the sake of designation.
Now, he states its function:
"Do not think of yourself as being devoid of breath; O fire-stick ascetic, do not bow toward the tip of the nose. (103) "Pāvana" means wind.
One will not perceive the self as being devoid of that which is characterized by inhalation and exhalation through the nose.
Why? As long as the body is dependent upon the vital air (*vāyu*), how can there be a location for the body once it is devoid of that [air]?
Thus, through the instruction of the Guru, having made the vital air consist of that [self], where are the selves not to be found?
Therefore, abandon with painful effort that attachment to her through conceptual yoga; this is the conclusion: "O fool, do not be attached to another while the innate [state] exists.
What is to be done? He says:
"O fool, be attached to the innate."
"Do not fall into the bondage of worldly existence.
Thus, O deluded man, you abandon the small-minded state; cultivate instead the great-minded state. What is that? Seek the innate. Upon entering that, exert your power through its vast significance.

"Do not have attachment to existence. The "smell of existence" refers to the state of being a *gandharva* (an intermediate being) due to the constant coming and going of births; do not form an attachment to that which arises from the impurity of the bonds of existence, like a whirling wheel. "Abandon this mind, as turbulent as a swift horse; it dwells in its innate nature and becomes motionless. Thus.
Such a mind and breath are exceedingly restless, like a horse; therefore, you must make them abandon that state through constant practice.
You will grasp this:
what is that natural state? It is the instruction of the Guru; by resorting to it, [the mind] will become directly motionless.
Because of the statement, "Merit and so forth are known by the self," he states its qualification: "When the mind's purpose is accomplished, O Jiva, the bond of the body is severed."
"In that [state] of equal flavor (*samarasa*) and the innate (*sahaja*), there is neither the outcaste nor the Brahmin.
Thus, at the very moment when the conceptualizing mind (*vikalpamanaḥ*) has set, all bondage perishes.
Not only does one's own bondage alone cease, but specifically at that time, for all people, there is the relinquishing of the innate state of equal flavor. (104)
In this way, all [deities] such as the five Tathāgatas of the families become inferior.
In whatever place other [deities] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara reside, all the worlds are dissolved and attached there, yet they do not become knowers of reality (*tattvavid*).
Therefore, for those who know the reality of all scriptures, [the worship of those deities] is fruitless without them.
And so it has been said:
"Among the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma of the Great Sage,
all those who do not truly know the reality are indeed fruitless."
Therefore he says:
"O son, you are well-established in the essence of the essence of grammar;
though you recite it, no one in the world has understood its purity. Thus.

"My son, just as you were lost when you did not recognize the extreme purity at the time of preparing the elixir of mercury (*rasarasa-āyana*), so too have you been lost by not recognizing the purity [attained through] passion and the like. Do not act in such a manner.
That which is play (*krīḍā*) with respect to the desired dharmas and so forth arising from passion is nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*), for it is thoroughly grasped as being devoid of reality."
It is not only regarding reality;
other people also provide explanations and recite [the scriptures],
yet for them all of it becomes fruitless.
Why? Because the world exists through ignorance regarding cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, for one who knows, it is said:
"O son, my disciple, it is not possible to describe the essence of that reality which has been contemplated;
there, the supreme world arises as a state of bliss free from conceptual construction.
Thus, O son, disciple, the taste of that reality which has been reflected upon cannot be expressed through the narrative of one's own experience.

This objective form, appearing in the shapes of blue, yellow, and so forth—likewise, how is it that it is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*), since he alone knows it? Therefore, it is free from conceptual construction (*kalparahita*) and is the locus of bliss, because its nature is the supreme reality of the world; this is the intended meaning. Thus, through meditation (105), it is not perceived [as an object] because it is established by its own nature (*svabhāvasiddhatvāt*); it is perceived merely through the thorough knowledge of the Guru, and not through pride and the like. He says this:
Where pride is shattered, the intellect perishes, the mind dies, and there is no conceit; in that supreme nectar of illusion, what meditation can be bound?

Thus, by the Guru’s imparting of the introduction to the *sahaja* (the innate), whatever fabricated intellect there may be is destroyed—that is, it is made to be forgotten—and the conceptualizing mind dies, characterized by external objects and the like.
In that state, conceit, egoism, and the conceptualization of "self" and "mine" are severed and go to destruction.
Because he is of the nature of the supreme *kalā* consisting of *māyā*, like the sixteenth *kalā*, he does not perform any function whatsoever.
Therefore, what need is there here for the bondage of meditation?
That is to say, it does not exist because it is mentally constructed.
He states its qualification:
"It arises from becoming and subsides through destruction."
"Furthermore, where is it produced when devoid of existence?
Thus, in that very place where what was consumed by worldly existence is once again free from decay,
he is likewise devoid of both existence and non-existence.
The meaning is that the arising of anything whatsoever is not tenable;
by this which has been stated, one does not become a nihilist.
Why? Because there is the consequence that everything characterized as the Buddha and so forth is like an illusion, being both existence and non-existence.
Rather, it is so called because of its association with conceptualization (*kalpanā*). Furthermore:
"The soul (*jīva*), having abandoned the body (*viṇṇa*), departs; it remains [in its true state], O Lord Guru, as is taught. Thus.

The intention is that among those pairs devoid of duality, one should practice yoga while being free from the perception of a middle; thus, [the state] between the supreme and the cessation is perceived by means of the middle.
Everything is indeed non-dual. Therefore, by abandoning even that, maintain that state.

Where the venerable Guru says "Do it with your head," this means the movement of the head itself, which is of a most wonderful nature. Therefore, by this principle, perform this circumambulation. (106)
"See, hear, touch, eat, smell, wander, sit, and stand.

Regarding these and other such [actions]: whatever you shall see here with the eyes, sounds you shall hear with the ears, clothing and the like for wearing, the body which moves, eating performed with ease, and fragrance with the nose—[all these belong to the Self].
Whether you smell a foul odor or wander about, whether you are seated on a seat or standing up—O Ālamāla, enough with worldly affairs! Abandon the mind; do not move even a single step. Thus.
Pass your time through such worldly dealings as buying and selling at Ālamāla;

yet, let your mind not waver from this non-dual yoga. Without being distracted by other thoughts, do not wander about with a nature of uniform form, conceiving yourself as a cause, an agent, and so forth;
for it is they who experience the sufferings of hell and other realms.

Therefore, remember the instruction of the true guru. Regarding him, it is said: "Those who have not drunk the nectar-like juice of the guru’s instruction run about like thirsty people in a desert of many scriptural meanings; they will die of thirst."

Those base individuals who, due to their state of being driven by great impetuosity, did not drink the nectar-like essence of the Guru’s instruction, have thereby failed in their purpose for all sentient beings. It is like this: in desert wastes, a caravan leader sees water at certain drying-up spots for a multitude of thirsty travelers; thinking that it has been brought there by a treasury-guardian, he does not inform the members of the caravan because they do not know him, and thus the entire company is brought to ruin.
In this way, through successive transmission, all sentient beings are brought to ruin.
Regarding the specific characteristic of the instruction, he says:
"Avoid both mind and non-mind; remain just as a child does."
If one possesses firm devotion to the words of the Guru, then the natural state becomes manifest;
[the mind] is without mind, being devoid of subject, object, and so forth,
and without intrinsic nature.
One should offer a remedy for those two; maintain a state like that of a child.
Cultivate firm devotion toward the Guru’s instruction alone, by which the manifestation of the innate arises.
And through uninterrupted practice, this recitation will become identical with that [reality].
And being identical with that, it is free from all obscurations and inexpressible; thus he says:
"The phonemes and letters are devoid of supreme qualities."
He says: "It is not known; thus it has been described.
By these two syllables (*akṣara-varṇābhyām*), that [reality] is not perceived.
Alternatively, *akṣara* refers to the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), and its *varṇa* is this description consisting of bliss, which is called ungraspable.
Thus, through a succession of words devoid of metaphor, you did not realize that he was such a person; for it was said by me in the *Saroruha*:
"Whatever conceptual construction arises in the mind, all of it is of a nature to be abandoned."
That which is of the nature of bliss and brings happiness to the heart is also merely a mental construction.
(108) Or rather, for the sake of detachment, even that duality is a cause for the non-grasping of the Self;
there is no other nirvāṇa anywhere than the state of being the non-conceptual Self.
Therefore, for this reason—
He is described as the Supreme Lord,
just as a maiden accepts her lover. Thus.

As long as the multitude of sentient beings remains in delusion, even though that Supreme Reality, the Supreme Lord, exists—since He is not present in other systems of tenets—to whom, indeed, who remains among ordinary people, shall I speak of Him?
For their engagement occurs through mere description.
Rather, it is like young maidens consulting with their female friends.
They reflect upon it and take it as a premise:
first, you went to your master and experienced happiness;
therefore, you speak of this directly to me—it is certain.
Having gone there and returned from his house, she asked her friend again what it was like as previously described.
They replied,
"It must be known by you at the time of direct experience with your husband."
There is nothing whatsoever that can be directly stated by you regarding the arising of bliss, because it is inexpressible.
Just as the instruction of a guru does not, however, establish the nature of an object as "the youth's pain," he says this very thing:
"He who is devoid of existence and non-existence..."
"In that, the entire world without exception is dissolved"— if this supreme reality is thus contemplated,

then because it is non-dual and devoid of the causes of existence and non-existence, the world— consisting of all Buddhas, Vajradharas, and so forth, as they are conceptually constructed— is dissolved therein; for, being identical with that, it is beyond apprehension.
"When the mind remains motionless there, one is liberated from the cycle of existence.

(109) According to the sequence stated here, if the mind is established in that state through immobility— because it is free from conceptual constructions such as "self" and "belonging to self"— then at that time, one becomes liberated from *bhava*, the defects of the transmigratory cycle of the six realms of existence.
Regarding this being done, he states the fault:
"As long as you do not recognize yourself as another, how can you attain the supreme state? Thus.

As long as you do not fully realize the Self, which is the supreme, most excellent, and essential reality (*tattva-rūpa*), how will you attain the unsurpassed reality of the body— the pervasive, constructed physical form (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)— since that [reality] is its pervader? Because it results in both unity and multiplicity, such a state arises for all due to the error of grasping at a self.
Why? Because it concerns the unsurpassed reality. Thus has this been told; it is not poetry. You must awaken the self by means of the self.
Such was spoken by me through the lotus; never entertain doubt regarding that. Through such doubt, you then perceive the self by means of the self.
Apart from this, nothing else exists at all. Therefore he said:
One should not contemplate atoms or even subtle particles; rather, by constantly meditating [on the Self], the state of supreme redness (surattatva) manifests.
Thus, atoms and subtle particles are not contemplated through meditative cultivation.

If it is made to flash forth through the cultivation of uninterrupted yoga and so forth, Saraha says: "O you who are intoxicated by this, how much more so! Thus, this indeed is merely knowledge consisting of conceptual construction.
By this yoga, doubt arises;
for I have not taught what is true reality. "O ṇikkolīs, understand the ultimate truth! Thus [it is said].
O fool, you are rootless, baseless, and without lineage;
you are devoid of the support for all seeds and so forth. Therefore, speak that ultimate reality. He said: "The supreme consciousness is rootless."
Meditation is rootless;
you are known as the rootless reality, for the Tathāgatas are indeed beyond lineage (*akula*).
Therefore, it flashes forth by its own nature, not by will, because of attachment to that—this is the meaning.
"He is at home, yet he asks about those outside;
he sees his neighbor, yet he asks about him.

Thus, for example, a certain man [sees] his own kinsman in the house of the Yoginīs, yet he asks outside, "Where is he staying? Then, seeing his beloved master standing nearby, he asks inside the house, "Where is he staying?"
Thus, [the opponent] asks: "The reality is established within one's own body, while that which is external is something else; what is knowledge?
[The answer is: "It is indeed nothing but ignorance."
Furthermore, by the instruction of the guru, he perceives and experiences his own direct experience (*svānubhava*).
Then, if someone standing nearby asks, "What is that reality?
he replies, "It is simply ignorance (*ajñāna*)."
That which is ignorance is what should be grasped;
since all phenomena are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), what is there to be known?
Thus, Saraha and others further establish this firmly—(111)—as follows:
Saraha says: "O fool, know the Self!
It is neither meditation nor concentration nor recitation.
Thus, understand all that which has been stated regarding reality by means of the Self within the Self.
Furthermore, that [reality] has been described according to its true nature in the form of meditation on the object of thought, dhāraṇā, and so forth.
As it is said: "If the Guru says that liberation is attained by knowing everything, can it be obtained by knowing everything? Thus.
Someone has said this: "Not everything that is taught by the gurus is understood [by the disciple].
When [the guru] speaks of that which is apart from the self, then he describes the nature of that object.
What is impossible for him? Liberation is what is obtained. Thus, when it is spoken by the gurus, one does not understand it due to transgression—that is to say, due to ignorance."
How, then, can it be known through practice? Because that [self] is grasped merely through habitual practice. He says this:
"One wanders in the country and takes up a dwelling;
one is not awakened to the innate by being seized by sin. Thus.
In this regard, there is a fault among those yogins who are base men:
having abandoned their own place, they wander through all lands;
for the sake of [distinguishing between] devotees and non-devotees, they do not know the exhaustion resulting from such physical suffering.
From what practice?
This very unsurpassed innate nature (sahaja) is neither known nor manifested.
Why? Because it has been seized by evil.
Regarding the phrase "from the Daitya who eats that":
the intended meaning is that it is devoid of practice.
(112) He performs [the action]. By that, a Śūdra does not become a specific caste such as a Brāhmaṇa; this is established.
The meaning is that all worlds are bound by a single birth and are indeed co-emergent (*sahaja*).
He states the consequence of this very point: "There is no philosophical conclusion (*siddhānta*) higher than the co-emergent. Thus:
"Here is the celestial river Yamunā; here is the Gaṅgā and the ocean."
"Here is Prayāga, here is Vārāṇasī; here are the Moon and the Sun.
Thus it truly exists as a perfect play. From where does this arise? It arises from its own innate self and the other-self through an uninterrupted flow.
That very [reality] is designated by names such as Yamunā and Gaṅgā, but not merely as a support for drinking water or bathing; rather, Yamunā is the refuge of all vehicles (yānas) and their basis.

The Gaṅgā is characterized by its flowing toward that [state]; the ocean represents the ocean of all instructions on meditative absorption (*samādhi*); Prayāga represents non-duality; Vārāṇasī represents the warding off of both duality and non-duality; and the moon and sun represent the eclipse by Rāhu. Thus, one should consume everything with the fire of instruction.
This applies not only to sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and so forth, but also to the natural seats (*pīṭha*), sub-seats (*upapīṭha*), and so on. He says this:
"Kṣetra, pīṭha, and upapīṭha are here"—
thus, all these twenty-four locations, beginning with kṣetra and upakṣetra,
constitute the task of the external circumambulation.
