And that [is expressed by] "maiṃ bhamai pariṭṭhao" (I wander, having established). The intended meaning is that, through the instruction of the Yoginī established by me while wandering, the entire universe—both external and internal—is nothing but bliss.
What, then, has been stated by this?
One's own body is of the nature of bliss; the manifestation of that element externally takes the form of sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth. Therefore, he says:
"The sacred seat (*tīrtha*) similar to the body—bliss is seen in nothing else.
If the sacred seat resembling the body is of the nature of bliss, then all is well.
When [the yogin realizes], "The sacred site (*tīrtha*) similar to the body has been easily attained by me," then the yogin should move about with non-differentiation from it.

Thus, furthermore, regarding the internal seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth, one should understand [the practice] through movement and the like; and in those [seats], the movement is by means of that which consists of bliss (*sukhamaya*), not by mere wind alone.
Therefore, it is established that the seats and so forth consist of the bliss of *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, for the perfected yogin who possesses the empowerment of the deities of the internal seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth, wandering to external seats and the like is purposeless. As it has been said:
"The twenty-fourfold divisions of the seats and so forth are established right here [within].
Therefore, those who perceive the ultimate reality should not undergo the exhaustion of traveling for the sake of grasping them."
"If for one devoid of reality there is nothing [real] due to the onset of delusion, then for those who are possessed of it, there is likewise nothing [real] due to that delusion.
Therefore, the conclusion is that its form is non-different. He says this:
"By means of the cluster, the bud, the petal, the lotus, the fragrance, the filament, and the excellent stalk"—by this illustration, abandon the notion of the lotus as a separate entity.

For it is not [a single thing] apart from each of its constituent parts, such as the cluster (*saṇḍa*), the bud (*puṇi*), the lotus leaf (*padmapatra*), the petal (*dala*), the lotus (*kamala*), the fragrance (*gandha*), the filament (*kesara*), and the excellent (*vara*) stalk (*nāla*). Thus—
Abandon the weaving; do not perform the drying; do not cling to the threads, O fool!
O beast-like person, abandon the separation from the aforementioned lotus;
cause the withering of the mind for each and every stage.
Therefore, do not become attached to such statements of ignorance through the various figurative usages found in different scriptures; for it is said:
"Ask one of low birth about the meaning of desire, in which the entire triple world, including Brahmā and Viṣṇu, is dissolved."
"What is the use of the mantra-śāstra that is external to the innate (*sahaja*)? Ask [this]: without those [mantras], the entire mantra-śāstra comes to ruin.
Just as when a father is absent, everything such as wealth belonging to a son who lacks noble lineage and is worthless comes to ruin and is seized by the king and others;
likewise, the entire mantra-śāstra or the Dharma comes to ruin when it is seized by ignorance through one who lacks the reality (*tattva*). Such is the collective meaning."
Having abandoned conceptualization like the innate space (*sahajākāśa*), by relying on primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), neither the Tathāgata nor anyone else obtains even a mere name;
in that state, everything comes to an end.
Thus, all five families of Tathāgatas and so forth become diminished.
In that place where others—such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the rest—are absorbed and attached, all the worlds become nothing for those who know the reality (*tattva*).
Therefore, for those who know the reality of all the scriptures, [all else] is fruitless without them.
Thus it has been said:
"Among the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma of the Great Sage,
those who do not indeed know the reality are all fruitless.
Therefore, he said:

"O son, you were lost because, while practicing the elixir of the essence (*rasarasa-āyana*), you did not know its true purity; likewise, the world is lost by those who recite [the scriptures] without knowing the purification of passion and the like. Thus, O son, just as you were ruined because you did not recognize the clear purity at the time of preparing the elixir of the essence, so too is the world ruined by failing to recognize the purification of attachment and other defilements.
Do not act in such a manner.

That play (*krīḍā*) with the objects of desire, such as the [five] dharmas, which arises from passion (*rāga*), is indeed thoroughly grasped as nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is devoid of reality (*tattva*).
This applies not only with respect to reality itself.
And other people provide explanations and perform recitations;
all of those becomes fruitless for them. Why? Because of their ignorance regarding the world of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, for one who understands,
it is said:
"O son, it is not possible to describe the object through various flavors."
The supreme world arises there as a state of bliss, perfected by time.
Thus, O disciple, son, it is impossible to describe in words the taste of that reality which has been contemplated;
for this form of things, consisting of blue, yellow, and so forth, is likewise self-cognizable, since he alone knows it.

Therefore, it is a state of bliss free from conceptual construction (*kalpa*), because its nature is that of the supreme reality of the world; this is the intended meaning. Thus, (115) it is not perceived through mental effort (*dhmāna*), because it is established by its own nature; rather, it is perceived merely through the thorough knowledge of the Guru, and not through pride (*abhimāna*) and the like. As it has been said:
"Where the intellect perishes and the mind dies, there pride is destroyed."
"Therefore, O Māyāmā, in that supreme state, what meditation can be bound?

Thus, by the Guru’s imparting of this introduction to the *sahaja*, whatever fabricated intellect there may be is destroyed and rendered forgettable; the conceptualizing mind dies, and in that state, there is no conceit regarding external objects, nor egoism, nor the mental construction of "self" and "mine"—all of which are severed and come to an end.
Since that [object] is of the nature of the supreme *kalā* consisting of illusion, it is like the sixteenth *kalā*, which does not perform any function;
therefore, what purpose is there here in the bondage of meditation?
That is to say, because it is a mental construction, it does not exist.
He states its qualification:
"In existence one accumulates; in destruction one exhausts.
But in that which is devoid of mental states (bhāva), how can anything be accumulated? Thus it is said.

In that state where what was consumed by existence is once again devoid of decay in this very place—thus being free from both existence and non-existence—further arising in any [other] place whatsoever is not possible; this is the meaning. By saying this, it is shown that he does not become a nihilist (*nāstika*).
Why?
Because it follows that everything characterized as a Buddha and so forth would be like an illusion, being both existent and non-existent.
What then? It is described as such because of its association with conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, in this way:
"Whatever practice one performs, avoiding the two [extremes], O Lord of the Great Gurus, it is explained:

'Abide!'—thus, among those pairs devoid of the two, the yoga is attained by means of the middle for those who are free from the perception of duality; the intention is that it is perceived through the middle between the supreme and the cessation."
"All is indeed non-dual. By abandoning even that [thought], maintain that state,
wherein you should receive the instruction from the head of the venerable gurus.
"It is indeed a most marvelous thing that the head itself moves.
Therefore, by this logic, perform this movement (?). (116) Look! Listen! Endure! Eat!

"Smell, wander, sit, and stand"—in these and other such [expressions], here you will see something with the eye; you hear sound with the two ears; you clothe the body with garments and the like; you eat food with pleasure;
you smell fragrance or foul odor with the sense of smell; you perform wandering or walking; you are seated on a seat or you stand up.
"Deal in *ālāmāla* transactions;
abandon the mind and do not waver in the state of oneness.
Thus, by means of such transactions as the buying and selling of *ālāmāla*, pass your time.

If this mind, through its union with non-duality, does not waver, you will not wander about in a single uniform state of being as an agent or a cause, independent of other minds. Because of that, they experience the sufferings of hell and so forth.
Therefore, remember the instruction of your guru. He says:

Those base individuals who, despite running with great speed, did not drink the nectar-like essence of the Guru’s instruction, have died of thirst upon the desert sands of the many meanings of the scriptures. By them, for the sake of all living beings, [the teaching] has been ruined.

Just as in desert regions, a caravan leader, seeing water in certain dried-up places where a great multitude was parched with thirst due to the lack of water, might think, "These have been deposited by a treasury-guardian," and not informing the caravan, causes the entire company to perish; in this way,
all sentient beings are destroyed through such a succession.
He states the specific characteristic of the instruction:
"Abandon both mind and non-mind, and remain just as a child does; through devotion shown toward the Guru's word, the natural state (*sahaja*) will arise."
"Mind" refers to cognition, the object of cognition, and so forth;
"mindless" refers to being devoid of intrinsic nature and so forth.
One should effect a resolution by means of these two.
Maintain yourself like a child;
cultivate exclusive and firm devotion to the guru’s instruction,
by which the awakening of the innate nature occurs.
And through uninterrupted practice, this manifestation will become identical with that [reality].
Being identical with that, it is free from all obscurations and inexpressible; thus he says: "Beyond syllables and sounds, devoid of supreme qualities."
He says: "I do not know; this has been told by me.
By these two syllables (*akṣara-varṇa*), that [reality] is not perceived.
Alternatively, *akṣara* refers to the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), and its *varṇa* (color/manifestation) is this bliss, which is described as being ungraspable.
Thus, through a succession of words devoid of metaphor, you did not understand that he was such [a person]; this was said by me, the Saroruha.
And so it has been said:
"Whatever conceptual construction arises in the mind, all of that is of a nature to be abandoned."

That which is of the nature of bliss and brings happiness to the heart is also merely a mental construction. (118) Or rather, for the sake of detachment, even that which is both [bliss and its opposite] is a cause for the persistence of worldly existence;
there is no other nirvāṇa anywhere in any object, because of the state of being the non-conceptual self. Thus.
Therefore—
That supreme lord is described as one who abandons even his own beloved,
just as a young maiden abandons her lover. Thus it is said.

As long as the multitude of sentient beings remains in error regarding their state of existence, I shall indeed explain that supreme reality to whom—that ordinary person established in a different system—since there is no other established doctrine?
For their engagement occurs through mere verbal instruction;
rather, it is like the way young maidens deliberate with their female friends.
They reflect and form a conviction:
"First, you went to your master and experienced happiness;
therefore, you speak of this directly to me—it is certain."
Having gone there and returned again from his house, she asked her friend what it was like as previously described.
They said,
"It must be known by you at the time of experiencing it directly with your husband."
He does not speak directly of the arising of bliss as something specific, because it is inexpressible;
he does not describe its nature as a concrete object, such as "the pleasure of a maiden," but rather like the instruction of a guru. This very point is stated:
"He who is devoid of both existence and non-existence..."
In that [reality], the entire world without exception is dissolved.

If this is to be contemplated as the supreme reality, it is because it is devoid of the duality of existence and non-existence due to their emptiness of cause; in that [state], the world—consisting of all the conceptualized forms of the Buddhas, Vajradharas, and so forth—is dissolved, for it is indistinguishable from that [reality].
When one's mind remains motionless,
at that moment one is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence (*bhava-saṃsāra*).

Thus, according to the sequence stated [above], if the mind is established there in a state of immobility— due to being free from the conceptualization of "self" and "mine"— then at that time one becomes liberated from *bhava*, that is, from the defects of the cycle of existence consisting of the six realms of rebirth.
Regarding this being done, he states the faults:
"As long as you do not recognize yourself as other, how can you attain the unsurpassed state? Thus.

As long as you do not fully realize the self as the supreme, most excellent, and essential reality, how could you attain the unsurpassed reality of the body—the physical form composed of the *nirmāṇakāya*—which is all-pervasive? Because it is pervasive, [the notion of attainment] arises as both one and many; therefore, for everyone, such a state results from the error of grasping at a self.
Why? Because it concerns the unsurpassed reality. Thus has this been told; it is not poetry.
You must awaken yourself by means of yourself.
Do not ever entertain doubt regarding what has been said by me, Saroruhā;
for through such doubt, you will then perceive yourself as something other than yourself.
Apart from this, there is nothing else at all. Therefore, he said:
One should not contemplate atoms or even the most subtle particles;
rather, when one contemplates the state of non-atomhood, the supreme redness (the nature of reality) flashes forth.
Thus, atoms and subtle particles are not contemplated through meditative cultivation.
"If it is made to flash forth through the cultivation of uninterrupted yoga and so forth," says Saraha: "O you who are intoxicated by delusion, this is but mere conceptual knowledge.
For this is indeed knowledge consisting of mental construction (*kalpanā*).
By this yoga, doubt arises; for what I have spoken is not the state of perfect realization. "O Ṇikkolī, awaken to the ultimate truth! Thus [it is said].
O deluded man, you are rootless, uprooted, and without lineage;
you are devoid of the support for all seeds and so forth. Therefore, speak that ultimate reality. He said: "The supreme consciousness is stainless."
The cultivation is stainless;
the reality to be known is stainless, for the Tathāgatas are indeed beyond lineage (*akula*).
Therefore, by its own nature it manifests through desire; due to attachment to that, there is "bliss" (*surata*). This is the meaning.
"He is at home, yet he asks about those outside; he looks out the window, yet his neighbor asks him.

Thus, for example, when someone asks a yoginī, "Where is your own kinsman who is at home? and she, seeing her beloved husband nearby, replies, "He is right here in the house," and then asks, "Where is he? [the meaning is that she does not know].
Thus, [the opponent] asks: "Is the reality established within one's own body, while that which is external is something else, namely knowledge? [The reply is: "It is indeed ignorance."
Furthermore, by the command of the Guru, he perceives and experiences his own direct experience (*svānubhava*).
Then, if someone standing nearby asks, "What is that reality?
he replies, "It is simply ignorance (*ajñāna*)."
That which is ignorance is to be grasped;
since all phenomena are unconditioned, what is there to be known?
In this way, he further establishes [the point] firmly.
"Saraha says: Know that the Self is the Veda; it is neither meditation, nor concentration, nor recitation. (121)
Know all that which has been stated regarding reality through the Self alone within the Self.
Furthermore, that reality has been described in the form of meditation, concentration, and so forth.
If the Guru says this, then know it all.
"Liberation is indeed attained even without knowing everything"—this has been said by someone. This implies that not everything taught by the gurus is necessarily known;
rather, when [the soul] is free from the self [of ignorance], it then manifests the true nature of reality.
"What is impossible for him? What liberation is obtained? She replied: "It was said by the teachers that [he does not know] due to transgression, meaning because of his lack of understanding.
How then is it to be known? Through practice; for he grasps the Self through mere practice. He says this:
"He wanders in the country and receives [instruction] from the fire-places."
"The innate [nature] is not understood due to sins;
thus, there is a fault here for those practitioners who are base men.
Having abandoned their own place, they wander through all lands."
Due to causes such as devotion or lack of devotion, they do not know the exhaustion resulting from physical mortification.
From what practice [could they know it]?
Thus, they neither know nor manifest this unsurpassed innate nature (*sahaja*).
Why? Because it is seized by evil;
that is, because of the non-duality of what is to be consumed.
The meaning is that it is devoid of practice. (122)
And so it has been said:
"Just as fire situated within wood does not arise without friction,
so enlightenment is not born in this life without practice."

Someone might have the doubt: "If practice is performed by means of this [meditation], then how is the abandonment of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth explained? To address this, he says: "The object delights, yet the object does not smear; it seizes the stomach, yet it does not touch the vital breath."* *Note: This verse appears in the *Paramārthasāra* (verse 103). The commentary explains that while the object of sense-enjoyment may appear to please the mind, it does not actually defile it;
though it may seem to satisfy the body, it does not truly affect the inner vitality.*

Just as foam is seen in the midst of water but the water itself is not grasped through the touch of the hand, so too, when there is such thorough knowledge, one may engage in play with sense objects such as the five desires, yet one is not affected by their defects.
Furthermore, just as a lotus leaf, having taken up the ripples of water, is not smeared by that water; [so too is the wise person].
And because of the statement, "That which has arisen is like a lotus leaf in water," such is the practice of the yogi: "In this way,
O yogi, flowing to the root..."
"One who delights in the objects of the senses does not overcome them.

Thus, for such a yogi—who, through practice, knows the source flowing from the river of the guru’s instruction—there is no affliction by those sense-objects; whatever among yogis takes the form of sense-objects and so forth, none of that ever becomes external to him.

What is knowledge, what is the object of knowledge, and what is the means of making it known? It is because [the Self] originates from that [knowledge]. Therefore, because it delights in all objects, it is not sublated; such is the meaning.
And so it has been said:
That which is external is non-existent because it is devoid of its own nature, and cognition is likewise like the external object;
that which is empty and unconstructed by the wise is nevertheless considered non-empty.
Having reflected thus and having reached certainty through the abundance of entities, one whose mind is fixed on the single reality—
"The Lord of Yogins, highly skilled in the many dramas of illusion, plays thus: 'O King, he is being crushed;
though seen by the hundred thousand, he is killing himself—what can be done? (123) Thus.
If, first of all, birth occurs in the form of a deity, then since that characteristic is seen as being accompanied by consciousness, at that time the self dies;
what will that deity do? It amounts to saying nothing at all. Therefore—
"This saṃsāra does not cease; without hope, there is no exit.
Thus [it is said]. Even if one perceives oneself as having the form of a deity, this saṃsāra still does not perish.
Why? Because for all sentient beings, there is an absence of the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*) and so forth;

that which is the activity within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) constitutes the nature of the *gandharva* being, and that itself is the "return," due to the perception of the previous [existence] and so on.
And because the deity is perceived through such cognition,
therefore saṃsāra does not perish;
the sense is that it revolves like a false mechanical potter's wheel.
However, even when that thorough knowledge exists, without the practice thereof, there is no escape from the cycles of existence (*saṃsāra*).
This very [knowledge] does not become the state of a deity merely through the instruction of a guru;
for it is precisely for this reason that practice is performed.
Therefore, there is no distinction in non-existence; that does not occur.
You have not even heard the mere report of the authentic instruction of the Guru; what then did he say?—“By the cessation of the mind through unblinking eyes.”
"By the obstruction of the heavy head, the wind is restrained.
By this [verse], that which is imagined by those of dull intellect as a conceptual instruction from the Guru does not occur.
Just as one whose eyes are motionless and fixed makes the mind dissolve into space and so forth, by that means the vital air (vāyu) becomes restrained.
"By the command of the illustrious Guru," and so forth, does not occur.
Why did he say this?— because "the wind blows, yet it is motionless by us."

"Does death occur at that time? No, indeed. (124) At the very moment when the yogi makes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) motionless by means of its vehicle, the wind—O deluded man, does death (*kāla*) occur at that moment?
Therefore, it does not happen.
He asks why it does not happen and says:
"As long as one has not entered the village of the objects of the senses, so long does the self shine forth at will. Thus.
As long as the group of sense organs and their objects does not produce attachment through those two, the yogi does not understand the teacher’s instruction.
And that attachment is overcome by means of inquiry, scripture, and reasoning.
Furthermore, since the nature of entities such as the self is not perceived through distinctions such as ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and so forth, how could it be seen through direct perception?
And delusion is indeed false by virtue of being a delusion;
yet, through the vision of conventional truth, it appears like an illusion.
Thus, the entire universe of the three realms is like an illusion; therefore, why is any attachment made toward it?
That is to say, it is not performed.

Furthermore, for the Lord of Yogins, the Guru’s instruction flashes forth not by mere will, nor without being fully cultivated; rather, through the very practice of that [instruction], it is remembered, and thus one destroys [the afflictions]—this is the certainty.
"Who enters such an uneven junction? (Aiseṃ visama sandhi ko paisai).
Whoever has [something] within, yet as long as it is not seen—such is the person characterized by the aforementioned description who enters into words of difficult construction.
For what purpose? Because for that person, the reality of the self and so forth does not exist within, and as long as it is not perceived.
What will that be?
In brief, there exists no entity consisting of the object to be produced and the producer.
There is neither an object to be produced nor a producer; existence does not exist at all in any way.
Through the state of the object of meditation and the meditator, a distorted form arises.
The abandonment of that [state] is not your nirvāṇa, nor does it arise through mere desire.
Just as this meditation of a lion is seen without desire due to the exhaustion [of effort], so it is. (125)
To those who did not know this, he said:
"The scholar expounds all the sciences;
yet he does not know that spring has grown within his own body."
"His learning has not been shattered by that [criticism];
nevertheless, being shameless, he says, 'I am a scholar.
Thus, scholars provide explanations upon various scriptures."
Merely the web of words, pursued solely for the sake of material wealth, is the cause for going to hell.
Failing to understand the instruction of a true guru, they do not realize that Buddhahood resides within the body.
Relying on mere syllables while remaining ignorant of the true nature of sound, they provide explanations devoid of the guru’s oral tradition.
They, being themselves ruined, ruin others as well. Why?

Because they have not been destroyed by the fact that [the self] has traveled through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) over a succession of many births, which is the cause of its repeated coming and going.
If it is argued that he nevertheless continues to wander in saṃsāra in the form of the great hells and so forth,
even so, for this very purpose, the teacher Kambala said:
"Phonemes, words, sentences, genders, and numbers..."
Because of the relationship between action and its factors, and because they are unreal, [the words] are non-expressive.
For a verse is led by three sentences through five quarters;
since the sentence is dependent on what is to be expressed, it becomes the *ḍākinī-samaya*.
When all phenomena that ought to be grasped have been rendered empty by the ancients,
why has this world been cast into the perilous straits of the cycle of words? When it should be said, "This is not that," who indeed would point to anything when questioned?
With his head turned clockwise and his hand bent here, he himself has rendered lightness manifest through the analogy of the stone-press;
both himself and the world have been [liberated] by means of sounds, by means of masses of words that extract from sound. (126)
Such is the detailed account.
Then, once again, she spoke shamelessly:
"I am a fool, though I consider myself wise."
"As long as one does not decay while living, one becomes ageless and immortal.
This is the illustration for the meaning stated by Anena.
If, for instance, in some case a person is not seized by old age and the like until the very end of life and death, then he attains the state of being ageless and immortal.
Thus, it is not seen anywhere [as eternal].
However, it is observed that because all living beings are seized by fever and other ailments, life indeed ends in death; this is the first point.

The second is as follows: just as the eight metals are dissolved merely by being treated with a mercury-born (*rasajāti*) elixir until it becomes a supreme elixir (*atirasa*), so too at the time of death, the nectar (*amṛta*) does not age within sentient beings, whereby one makes them free from old age and death.
From the very beginning, the yogi whose mind is stainless [attains this] through consumption and other means until it is digested.
To the question "By what does one reach the state beyond old age and death?", he says:
"Only some rare person becomes truly fortunate through the instruction of the Guru."

He who, through the instruction of a true guru, has by means of a pure intellect accomplished the state of being ageless and immortal— having brought about the cessation of all defilements (*sāsrava*) through the fourfold division of the bodies of Dharma, Enjoyment, Emanation, and Great Bliss—
that person alone performs this and no other; therefore,
the sense is that such a person is fortunate and supreme.
"One who does not delight in sense objects that are pure, but wanders in absolute emptiness—
just as a bird that flies up with the hope of catching grain nevertheless falls back down.
Thus, he who, by the command of the Guru, does not take pleasure in the enjoyment of the five senses and so forth within the pure sense objects, thereby attains the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
Due to being separated from that [wisdom], he wanders in a state of absolute isolation, practicing only the mere enjoyment of sense objects within the sphere of emptiness.
Thus, he wanders in mere emptiness and accomplishes nothing at all.
Like a crow that, having alighted upon a ship in the middle of the ocean, flies up and then finds no other place to land, he remains there [stuck] once more. (127)
It falls right back there.
In this way, those of a childish nature fall into saṃsāra through the karma of saṃsāra. Another [falls] because of not seeing emptiness and because of taking recourse therein; therefore—
"O fool, do not create bondage through attachment to sense objects;
listen to what the wise have said regarding fish, deer, elephants, bees, and deer.
Thus: do not create bondage by means of the enjoyment of the five sense objects and so forth.
This has been stated with effort by me, Saraha:
if you act [thus], then there is destruction— like a fish desiring the water of its longing when it is powerless,
or like a moth clinging to form that meets its destruction in a lamp.
The elephant meets its destruction by touch;
the bee meets its destruction by scent;
likewise, the herd of deer meets its destruction by sound.
Behold it yourself!
For that [consciousness] arises preceded by passion (rāga) in all beings;
O Lord, wherever the mind expands, there You are present in Your true form.
In those [beings], where a mental projection (*visphurita*)—such as going, eating, or other actions—is conceived, there is no intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) therein.
Why? Because it is unknown.
From what [is it unknown]?
Due to the deception of hunters, fishermen, and others, as well as through the ignorance of lustful men, beings are killed by the servants of Yama and similar agents.
Furthermore, out of extreme compassion, the author has stated:
"What else is the ocean? What else is the water? The nature of existence is like space."

Just as the water in a river is nothing other than the waves themselves, so too, because existence (*bhava*) is essentially pure, it is of the very nature of peace (*śānti*), which is identical to the nature of space (*khasama*); it is not something else.
What is expressed by this?
That which is existence is itself *nirvāṇa*, according to the knowledge of the wise through the correct instruction of the Guru.
The ignorant do not know; they go toward sense objects.
Such knowledge as this—whom shall it be told? Who here will listen? Everyone is absorbed in their own affairs.
Like dust from a well-constructed tunnel, that which is born of the heart is dissolved within the heart.
(128) Thus it is said. To what ignorant person is this most profound path described?
Who here is that man worthy of being told [this], or who, having skillfully grasped his place among these tasks, proceeds to that state and never falters?
"A worthy recipient indeed. Rare are those bulls among men who are excellent recipients.
Just as, for instance, a tunnel is constructed deep underground and far away in order to break through a dam.
That [place] is accessible only to those with excellent subterranean passages, not to others.
Why? Because there, for the purpose of digging through narrow openings, there is extremely noxious dust;
by which those of small heart meet death at that very moment.
And because the hearts of the tunnel-dwellers are much firmer, that dust merges into their hearts;
the clay, however, merges into the earth,
because at the initial commencement, a small portion of the combustible material has been left behind.
Thus, for those who have practiced in previous births, enlightenment within the great cycle of existence is for the sake of the essential heart-meaning alone; this is the intended sense.
He states its qualities:
"In whatever way it enters the water of the ocean, it becomes of the same flavor as that."
O friend, there is no one who can distinguish between faults and virtues through mere thought; for just as water mixed with water in the oceans attains a state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*),
so too, when faults and virtues such as those of *saṃsāra* are contemplated by a person of great psychic power (*maharddhika*) who possesses full knowledge, they do not become his adversaries.
From where do the defects arise, such as the qualities of the five sense-pleasures?
Their purification is brought about by the various words of the Guru through uninterrupted recollection, just as the water of a river is purified by its continuous flow.
He speaks again of its clarity:
"Form an attachment to emptiness; wherever you do so, contemplate it as equal.
Even a pain the size of a sesame husk will inevitably cause suffering.
Thus, one should not form an exclusive attachment to emptiness, by which annihilation would occur.
Contemplate equality among all things in their various natures, not only within yourself;
if you thus bring yourself and others— the entire universe— into a state of oneness (due to the absence of plurality), there is no fault.
Just as even within a single sesame seed there is a husk,
and within that husk there is a dark speck; that is a thorn, and by means of it, it inevitably causes pain.
Thus, for the lord of yogis, emptiness becomes a thorn by means of mere mind;
a state of well-being in all limbs is not attained.
If neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, neither duality nor non-duality is cultivated, then what is to be cultivated? To this he says:
Such a thing does not exist as something other than this, just as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) is like its effect.
Thus, such a thing— whether in the form of blue, yellow, and so forth, or in the nature of experience— is merely a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa).

[If it is asked: "How is it known that such a state—possessing both the conceptualization of perception and non-perception, and the conceptualization of mind and non-mind—is devoid of all bases, seeds, and supports?
[The answer is: It becomes like the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) in accordance with its function.
Just as no object whatsoever is seen anywhere from the wish-fulfilling gem, [so too is this state].
Furthermore, even when it has come into one's hands, a dull-witted person still harbors doubts regarding all matters;
likewise, for yogis as well, the instruction of the Guru—like a jewel already held in the palm—is not realized as Buddhahood and so forth merely by wishing for it. This is the intended meaning.
He now describes the conduct of those who are learned but do not understand this:
"Destroyed is the wise man, ruined by delusion regarding the mere letter 'a';
he has been made to dwell in the great bliss of self-awareness.
Thus: "Akkaṭa" means "wonderful"; the wise man, relying on a mere phoneme, was destroyed by delusion.
That is to say, it has not been destroyed.
Why? Because self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), which is included within all phenomena, is perceived equally.
That is to say, it is non-perception.
By that delusion, through this explained state of mind and non-mind, this characteristic of self-awareness was described in terms of great blisses [attained] through the touch of external women.
Furthermore, they spoke of the explanation of the very firmness of that same external great bliss:
"Therein, every form is made equal to space."
"The mind should be held in a nature equal to space.
(130) Whatever object, such as form and so forth, is made equal to space within that [state],
and the mind is maintained through its own nature which is equal to space— for that purpose—

Thus, that mind which is like the sky is rendered non-mind by its own innate nature; it rejoices in that very state. In this way, even that mind, whose true form is equal to space, is made non-mind within that [state].

Thus, he who acts in this way is the Supreme Person; he delights and plays within the innate natures (sahaja-svabhāva). Thus, in every house this pure narrative is told; yet it has not been heard by others—that state of great bliss.
Thus, with their contemptible intellects,
they speak in every house for the sake of deceiving sentient beings.
Such is this "pure exposition" by which, through your discourse, [the world] shall become pure from this day forward.
Therefore, that which carries [the meaning] is something else entirely; perform the realization of abiding in great bliss through another, superior explanation.
Thus, it is said: "Therefore, the Purāṇa alone is the [true] destruction. And so it has been stated:
He saw him fashioning garlands from sky-flowers while looking at footprints in a waterfall,
and weaving a cloth without thread.
"How indeed does the world not feel shame?"—
with this lamentation regarding the faults of those who are contemptible, the author says "Sarahan speaks," and so forth: "The world is afflicted by its own mind."
That state is without mind (*acitta*) and cannot be grasped by anyone.

Thus, by my instruction, the entire world of fools—including those who are "foolish-scholars" (*mūḍha-paṇḍita*)—has been led away and brought under control through the various modes of "mind" and "non-mind" as previously described. You abandon that mind; for it does not truly exist in the form of "non-mind."
Why? Because that which is characterized by non-mind has not been caused to be grasped by any mental procedure.
For what reason, then, does that which is of the nature of non-mind—such as wood, stone, and so forth—possess self-awareness?
In this way, how is such a form of non-mind characterized?
It means that it is not perceived;
because that [reality] is the very nature from the very beginning, and it is said: "The one God appears as many in the various scriptures."
"It appears clearly by its own will.
Thus, we observe that form of a single deity exists merely as a designation within many scriptures and their respective philosophical systems;
and it manifests clearly through the very will of the Self.
There is no other.
And so it is said in the glorious *Hevajra*:
"He himself is the sustainer, he himself is the destroyer; he is the king, he himself is the lord," and so forth. And he—

"The self has no other master; it is well-known in every house as the established doctrine that sorrow [is its lot]. Thus, by not desiring "self" and "belonging to self," there is destruction [of suffering] through the abandonment of base conceptualizations and attachments.
Furthermore, because it causes the cessation of other entities, this contradiction would not exist;
for this established doctrine is well-known in every house.
Why? Because it brings about the dissolution of what has arisen.
If, first of all, there is dissolution, of what is there arising?
And if there is arising, what is there dissolution? Therefore, both are unreal; for that reason, it was stated as such.
Such is the disposition of distinguished yogins.
For those established therein, this knowledge arises spontaneously from the instruction of the guru;
for one who does not possess it—(132)
He does not receive the guru’s instruction;
for this is not approved by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding them, it was said by the Blessed One in the Hevajra:
"For the entire world has its origin in me; the three worlds have their origin in me.
All this is pervaded by me; no world is seen that consists of anything else.
This states an example of those who are contemptible:
"One eats, while another also swells; she goes outside and rolls about before her husband.
Thus, when someone consumes food and other such things [in this manner].
One [type of person] effects the dissolution of food and sustenance into another because of its lack of commonality;
just as yogis consume it as a single substance.
Another, moreover, will even speak with lamentation for those who desire to eat.
Furthermore, the wife, having left her own husband and gone outside the house, beholds another man;
this is because of the multiplicity of minds [in the case of the ignorant], whereas for the knower there is a state of oneness through the form of knowledge.
Such is not the case for the ignorant.
He finds contentment in one thing alone; he knows only that one, not the manifold. Even those of dull intellect possess such a mind, yet by it they are lost.
While He is coming, He is not seen; while He is staying, He is not perceived.
The Supreme Lord is without waves [of agitation] and stainless; thus He is meditated upon. Thus it is said.
In accordance with the preceding verse, such a lack of understanding is described even among the wise:

just as a wife feeds her husband in her own home, yet also inquires about the food and so forth of another husband, and having departed from her own home, tests her husband; therefore, though he is present she does not see him, and though he has gone she will not see him. (133)
Even while remaining in his own home, he does not perceive it.
Such knowledge, being waveless, allows him to grasp the Supreme Lord according to his own will—flawless and free from all exertion.
What would be the result of this statement?
In this case, innate knowledge arises for the Yoginīs born of the field (kṣetraja) and so forth; yet she does not know anything [of the external world],
but perceives through her identity with that [knowledge].
"It was done by me; it was produced by me," and so forth, in detail.
It is to be understood exactly thus through the instruction of the Guru. Furthermore:
"As long as one does not abandon [the world], for that long..."
"O unprecedented playful woman, attain [this]!
Thus they come and go; she, the mistress of the household, does not abandon them.
This is well-known in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) such as Kāmarūpa and others: just as a certain man, staying at home, causes another person to go to a different place and returns from halfway there.

In the same way, by the power of the knowledge of the Yoginī—what does this do? It is explained: even while traveling, in whatever place he may be, he obtains union with an unprecedented beautiful woman.
Then, by that [means], he causes injury to the mind;
that is to say, such a thing as a previously unknown beauty is not obtained anywhere.
He asks, "What is appropriate? and says:
"The mind shines, given without support; do not see the three forms as distinct.

Thus, by the Yoginīs, the pleasant mind is to be beautified; the house of the shadow of the jewel placed in the forehead is to be known as non-dual awareness, wherein the non-duality of body and pleasure arises.
"Of a single form" (ekarūpa)—up to this point. For this very reason, he will say:
"Just as the eye and other [senses] exist as distinct from form, even though they exist in that way, you will not see form as something separate."

Why? Because from the binding of the thread and so forth, there arises a state of uniformity; therefore, the distinct forms of female and male, when permeated by knowledge, become non-distinct like the thread.
In this very way, the knowledge of yogins arises from their own nature; it is not produced by that [knowledge].
And by them, the accomplishment of all purposes is not achieved through mere will. As it is said:
"As long as the body, speech, and mind are not dissolved, so long one does not delight in the innate nature."

By this [means], as long as the body, speech, and mind of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) have not been differentiated and melted through the grace of the Guru, so long will there be no cessation of the defiled phenomena (sāśravadharmāḥ).
Consequently, they remain attached to those innate natures (sahajasvabhāva),
whereby the unsurpassed system of the Yoginīs is attained.
To the question "What then is the system of the Yoginīs?", he says: "In whatever place there is no consideration, there the housewives eat in the house."

"In whatever place the householder eats, and his own home is located—in such places as these thrones and so forth, we see [him]. This is imagined by ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) without investigation, not by the lords of yogins (*yogīndra*); he speaks of their state of being:"
"O Mother, why has the conduct of the Yoginīs been forgotten there?
(135)" [This means: Where the master of the house has been killed, there is no ritual service (*upacāra*) for another;
however, the ritual service performed toward others is supreme, as this consists of the nature of the Self in the form of the Lord of the Yoginīs.
It was seen to have been killed and eaten by others who were contemptible;
however, by the Yoginī with the "skin-eye," it was neither killed nor eaten.
The meaning is that it was made to consist of the Innate (sahaja), to be of the nature of the Innate, and to be dissolved into the Innate.
Therefore, the conduct of the Yoginīs is entirely dissimilar from all scriptures and worldly conventions.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"One eats in the house, one delights in the innate (sahaja), and one performs both attachment and detachment."
"Sitting by my side, the yoginī appears to me as a fallen woman.

When the householder has been devoured [by the demon], she is again colored by her innate nature; she experiences passion and dispassion, takes refuge with another husband, and laments both passion and dispassion.
She grieves for her former husband.
And by standing at the side of her own beloved,

that Yoginī appears thus in the mind as if devoid of mind, like my own state as a lord of yogis. Thus, the aggregate of the Yoginī’s gnosis, due to its non-duality, does not produce an appearance as an object of action.
He is not afflicted by the extremes of action and non-action;
for him, that [state] is merely an appearance to ordinary beings.
Furthermore, everything arising from the mind is conceptual construction; by means of this, that Lord of Phenomena, whose body is dependent upon his own mind, has consumed it.
The mind is the body, consisting of the seats (pīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha), and so forth. For yogis, these are the primordial natures (prakṛtis).
Through the cessation of that [mind], there is the cessation of the primordial natures.
What is perceived then?
One should know it through the instruction of the Guru. Having established this, the following is explained.
"Eat, drink, do not worry; let it appear in the mind.
O mind, you who are difficult to perceive, alas, this is the deceptive nature of a yoginī!
(136). Whatever action is performed—such as eating or drinking—one should do whatever appears to the mind; however, it is not done by the mind itself.
What is the use of that which is difficult to perceive through logic for one who possesses the knowledge of the Yoginīs? As before, it remains latent.
When the path of the dissimilar Yoginī is resorted to, everything becomes well-established; it is not otherwise. He speaks again:
"O Night, today is the day of the three worlds, by whom [it] is measured."
Thus,

he who knows the day and the night, for whom the three worlds are a manifestation free from the fear of [ordinary] perception— he is one who has attained the perfection of mind (*cittasiddhi*); he possesses the knowledge of the *yoginī*sahaja-saṃvara*, or rather, he realizes it directly.
To those who do not understand this, he says:
"The entire world is supported by syllables, yet there is nothing that is without syllables;
therefore, one churns with syllables until one arrives at that which is without syllables."
Thus, while remaining unimpaired, the entire world is bound by the notion:
"This is yours," "This is mine," or "This is a jar," "This is a cloth"—as spoken by the learned.
This is practiced throughout one's life, yet the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is not realized; nothing at all is accomplished.

What is this "without syllables" (*nirakṣara*) by which Buddhahood is accomplished? It is that very same syllable which, when melted through cultivation, crushes the entire web of speech produced by falsehood; as long as it proceeds toward the state of being without syllables, it is not truly "made. What supreme state does it then attain? To this he says:
"As it is outside, so it is inside; he stands without interval throughout the fourteen worlds. (137) "Whatever is the external nature of the lords of yoga, such is their internal nature."
Rather, it is because it consists of the form of knowledge (*jñānākāra*).
It abides in those fourteen worlds with a continuous, uninterrupted front, due to the absence of the supreme *kalā*.
And that yogi, being bodiless, is like the digit of the moon at the end of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Therefore, he said:
"The bodiless one is hidden within the body; he who knows it therein is liberated therein. Thus:
when the bodiless reality is directly set at rest within the sentient being, he by whom that knowledge is realized becomes liberated in that state.
Why? Because the world is one who experiences within themselves; and that which is to be experienced has not arisen at all from the very beginning, because it lacks a body.
This knowledge is formless.
Its designation is "the occurrence of bliss" (*sukhapravṛtti*).
That is the innate (*sahaja*) nectar.

For persons and individuals, at the time of their prior arising and destruction, there is no abiding in bliss within that very [state], because it is not a place of stability; rather, it is dissolved right there.
Therefore, the prior state of formless cognition is itself designated as the *dharmadhātu* and so forth.
Thus, whoever understands this through the teacher’s instruction becomes liberated in this very life with this very body; it is not otherwise.
When this has been stated, the author, because of his transformation into that [state], does not see any other [object]; therefore, expressing this, he says:
May there be success! This was recited by me for the first time.
While drinking the cream, this measure escaped my memory; here, I have understood but a single syllable.
"I do not know her name; this is certain.

(138) Just as in childhood, when for the sake of learning the alphabet one studies everything from "May there be success on the writing boards" onwards—up to grammar including the *Sūtradhāra* and so forth, as well as logic (*tarka*), Mīmāṃsā, and the rest—at that time, no fruit whatsoever was seen in any of those letters because of ignorance.

Furthermore, while striving to please a virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), I reflected through thorough investigation: that first phrase, "May there be success" (*siddhir astu*), is the truth; everything else I have recited is essence-less syllables.

Just as when cooking rice, the essence is taken [first], a practitioner (*samayin*) drinks the solid grain (*khaṇḍa*), yet considers the remaining husks (*maṇḍa*) to be the essence; having drunk that, he forgets the other and grasps only the thought, "May there be success.
It is this single syllable alone—the aforementioned knowledge—that has been realized by me here.
In that regard, because it is inexpressible, I do not know what the name of "the beautiful" (*vāmasya*) is like; yet, let there be the accomplishment of the meaning.
Nevertheless, even in its state of maturity, there is no manifestation of names, letters, and so forth.
Others of dull intellect do not understand this; regarding them, he said:
"In the state of *rūpaṇa*, all yogis find no entry;
it is explained as the great bliss in the hollow of the *kunduru*. Thus.

By means of the form of the innate (*sahaja*), that which falls within the entire triple world is not grasped, nor is it even expressible by name through the aspect of self-arisen gnosis (*svayaṃbhū-jñāna*).
Yet, at that time, they themselves are destroyed and cause others to be bound as well.
What is that? It is the claim that one accomplishes great bliss (*mahāsukha*) during the moments of sexual union (*kundurūkṣaṇa*).
Therefore, those embodied beings are fools.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Just as a thirsty deer runs toward a mirage,"

He dies of thirst; where can he obtain water from the sky? (139) Just as one afflicted by thirst, out of blindness caused by extreme thirst, runs upon seeing what appears to be water, yet his eye perceives only mist and not water—then, due to that affliction, he dies of thirst. Where can water from the sky be obtained? The meaning is that it cannot be obtained.

In this very way, reality is not attained through the practice of *kunduru* (mercury/alchemical elixirs). How could reality be known by foolish people, or what logic could there be for it? He says this very thing: "The elements, the earth, the self, the senses, and the objects of the senses are all devoid of [intrinsic] existence."
"In the *dohā* meter, *ṇau* and *ṇau* [occur], yet nothing is ever hidden.

Thus, one perceives that which has the nature of the delusion of conceptualizing the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), faculties (*indriya*), and objects (*viṣaya*).
In that state, neither the characterized (*lakṣya*) nor the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) exists; within all these, the world is perceived as the notion of water in a mirage.

And the state of water does not exist at all; it is merely through the perception of the appearance of a mirage that the delusion of a mirage is cognized as the appearance of water. Therefore, reality is shown by the word *anyānya* (the ever-new and other).
Within this *dohā*, and among all the *dohās*, nothing has been kept secret nor has the Guru’s instruction been destroyed;
for this purpose, he says he seeks forgiveness from all the learned: "O learned ones, forgive me much; let no doubt be raised here."
"What I have heard from the words of the Guru, how can I describe that which is so well-guarded?

Thus [it is said]. O learned ones, such knowledge—both hidden and revealed—has been told by me; therefore, grant me your forgiveness. Why? Because it was not kept secret in a place where secrecy was required, but rather, with a mind intent on benefiting sentient beings, it was disclosed even in a place where it should have been kept secret. Therefore, one should not entertain any doubt regarding this; this is indeed the consensus.
"It does not belong to me alone.
Why? Because even for me, what kind of speech was heard from my own guru—both that which is well-guarded and that which is manifest?
What would be gained by speaking thus?"

"Hidden among worthy beings"—this very point he expresses as follows: (140) "He who dwells in the center of both the lotus and the thunderbolt is the play of divine love. Who in the three worlds would delight in him? And whose hope would he not fulfill? Thus.

By this, the Blessed One has shown that for those who are absolute beginners, or for those with weak yoga, or for those attached to passion, the very play of great passion (*mahārāga*) is the means (*upāya*) to Buddhahood.
Likewise, what playful dalliance in sexual union (*surata-vilāsa*) has been introduced here by me within the pair of the lotus and the vajra—what heroic man would not delight therein?
By that, whose desire in the three worlds has not been fulfilled?
Because all [beings] consist of that and possess its intrinsic nature, the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) is fulfilled for all;
this is the rule because of the manifestation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
However, it is not so for those of superior faculties.

What is that? It is said: if reality (*tattva*) were [realized] by means of the lotus and vajra, then, having produced bliss for oneself, if one departs without the experience of bliss for another, that [reality] would not have fulfilled the entire triple world;
it would be merely the gnosis of a Buddha (*buddhajñāna*).
Therefore, such a gnosis of a Buddha is not the awakening (*abhisambodhi*) in a single moment for all [beings], because [the realization] of all would occur simultaneously. In brief:
The moment is indeed auspicious, or rather, both are auspicious;
by the grace of the Guru’s feet, if it is meritorious, perhaps someone rare may understand it.
This is a moment of happiness, distinguished from the four types of moments.
Alternatively, one may discern the reality even within an undivided moment;
and that [moment] is indeed undivided between the supreme (*parama*) and the cessation (*virama*).

At the first commencement, in the moment of the variegated (*vicitra*) and so forth, it is undivided from the state of production; by the grace of the Guru’s feet and through the power of merit, that very [state] is the innate nature (*sahaja-bhāva*).
Since only some rare individuals among people know [this] in some place, it is not common to all sentient beings.
Therefore, by means of the instruction of a true guru and according to the logic previously stated, I have made this manifest as something common to all people. And thus—(141)
"Through profound examples, neither another nor oneself [is realized];
through the state of naturalness (*sahājanda*), one knows the four moments and one's own spiritual urgency (*samvega*).
Thus, that which rare people know regarding meritorious deeds is established by closing off both sides and non-sides through the power of deep reflection and constant mindfulness.
In that which is supremely profound, there is neither another nor a self, nor anything at all,
because it is devoid [of such things] from the very beginning.
Such is one's own self-awareness, which you shall know in the fourth moment through innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) amidst the constructs of the world.
Indeed, he alone knows them once again.
He states its benefit:
"Just as a moonstone produces light in a terrible, pitch-black darkness,"
"The supreme great bliss removes all defects in a single moment.
Thus, in this midst of terrible darkness, it acts as an illumination like a moonstone (candrakānta-maṇi);
it is such that it cannot be taken away by any thieves, outcasts, or the like.
Such supreme great bliss (*paramamahāsukha*) eliminates the entirety of the misdeeds of *saṃsāra* in a single moment. Thus it is said:
"When the sun of suffering has set, the moon of bliss arises;
even by him who remains in the state of the unconstructed (*nirmāṇa*), the circle of the maṇḍala was fashioned."
Just as when the sun, the source of suffering during the summer season, sets, it brings about extreme coolness;
then the moon, the leader of the host of stars, and Venus arise.
Such is the circle of the maṇḍala and so forth—(142)
Meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is performed;
by means of that which abides as an emanation, one emanates the universe as an emanation through the conventional reality of a Buddha.
The essential meaning is that its own-nature is to be understood as the mandala-circle.
Furthermore, he states what must be done by yogins:
"O mind, O mind, sleep! O fool, abandon all false views.
When purified in supreme great bliss, perfection is attained therein. Thus it is said.
You examine mind with the mind;
however, both mind and non-mind exist.
By the very reasoning previously stated, neither of the two exists. And so it has been said:
In this world, it is only the mind that is not accumulated, for due to the absence of duality there is nothing whatsoever.
Indeed, nothing at all exists; this entire world is known through delusion.
Therefore, you abandon and relinquish all wrong views.

All such things as the self (ātman), the individual soul (jīva), the person (puruṣa), and the person-entity (pudgala) are merely conventional designations for base worldly transactions; they have been described as such. Purify all these within the supreme, great bliss.

By means of which one enters into the supreme stage, the supramundane, and the Buddha-concealment (*saṃvṛti*), for him there arises the most excellent and supreme accomplishment in the long term; therefore, this [is said]:
"In liberation, there is no conceptual differentiation of the mind-stream; here, indeed, there is no doubt."
The sky, the mountains, and the river water are enjoyed there; one dwells on their banks at will.
Thus, O lordly elephant whose mind is liberated, sport as you desire within the midst of saṃsāra.
You do not ask about this conceptual distinction.
Why? Because all phenomena are of the nature of reality, dependent upon reality, and dissolved within reality;
yet you avoid such evil deeds as the taking of life.

By those [such as] the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and others, one goes to hell; whereas by the compassionate ones, through the preservation of the ten paths of wholesome action, everything becomes well-situated.
Therefore, like an elephant, one drinks the water in the river while pervading all things with that mountain of space (gaganagiri).

The meaning is this: that person who, from that very place, dries up the river of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) at its banks—even within that great bliss, it is merely conceptualization (*vikalpa*); such is the nature of its confluence. As it is said:
"Just as one might seize a deer with a snare and kill it."
Just as a yogin emerges from his disguise, so too does he depart;

yet, while seizing all objects among the lordly elephants of the sense-objects—such as the eyes and the rest—as if an elephant were grasping with its trunk, it then appears like a slaughter. [As long as this appearance persists, for whom is there a subject and what is the object?]
This is its very nature that is perceived;
no killing is performed, nor is one led to the hells and other realms.
Such is the case for the lords of yoga, appearing exactly as it will through edible food and the like.
Having emerged from that [state] as if it were such [an object], he proceeds;
he dissolves into the innate [consciousness]. It is not [matters] such as edible food that afflict him; for him, it is merely the appearance of the world.

Thus, he is not defiled by what is edible or inedible; as it has been said: "That which is existence is indeed nirvāṇa; do not consider them to be different. One who has attained a stainless intellect perceives them as non-distinct from the single nature."

Thus, there is no distinction among yogins; this is the summary. As it was stated by the noble Nāgārjunapāda in the *Yuganaddhakrama* with the words "existence and nirvāṇa," and so forth, here too it is precisely this: existence and nirvāṇa indeed [are one]. (144)
In all dualistic expressions, there is a pair consisting of the knowable and the coupled [means and goal], and that is distinct from the knowable.
What then? That which is non-dual by virtue of its single nature is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in all scriptures; therefore, it is not devoid of the state of being both one and many.
However, when even this non-duality is realized as stainless, that is the sense of "supreme non-duality" (*paramādvaya*).
To clarify this very point, he says:
"Do not stay at home, nor go to the forest; wherever you are, there is the path and its practice.
Everything is continuously established in awakening; where is saṃsāra, and where is nirvāṇa?"
By this [statement], they do not remain in their own homes;
nor should they go even to another forest.
What then? A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises regarding which of two certain places is to be gone to.
How is this performed? It is said:

Having stood in whatever place, or having performed walking, eating, and so forth, perform the mental cultivation (*paribhāvanā*) therein; make that mind false and make it non-informative (*avijñapti*).
And that has already been refuted previously because it is unestablished (*asiddhatva*).
Therefore, because its stream flows without interruption or separation throughout all the three realms,
it is established as abiding in enlightenment;
it has not been produced by anyone, owing to its self-existent nature.

Therefore, in this matter, why would that which has been imagined by the dull-witted through delusion not apply to the non-duality of existence and nirvāṇa, even according to the reasoning already stated?
Nirvāṇa does not exist in that [existence]. Why? Because since there is no arising of the universe from the very beginning, why is it perceived at all?
"Like an illusion" means that it appears solely as a mere manifestation due to delusion.
Just as a reflection is seen in mirrors and the like, yet is not found upon investigation,
so too [the object] is impossible because of its lack of identity with the dimensions and other qualities of the original object.
Why is there the impossibility of both existence and nirvāṇa?
Thus it has been said:
"Those who do not see reality as it is conceive of both nirvāṇa and the world."
Those who see reality do not conceive of either the world or nirvāṇa in this way;
for both nirvāṇa and existence—this duality—does not exist. The thorough understanding of existence itself is called nirvāṇa. (145)
Therefore, the supreme non-duality, whose nature is awakening, is established; and he said: "Know this distinction: it resides neither in the boat nor in the house, nor in the forest.
By means of the nature of the stainless mind, accomplish the complete state of peace. Thus.

This is for the sake of illustration: enlightenment does not abide in the house nor in the forests. Thus you understand this distinction even within the context of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*): "house" refers to the body and "forest" refers to jars, cloths, and so forth; therein there is no enlightenment. Why? Because [enlightenment] is impossible in all such things.
Thus, whatever differentiation such as the world and so forth is perceived, all that is subject to arising and destruction;
enlightenment is not like this, because it is indestructible.
Therefore, one here effects the state of having a mind whose intrinsic nature is stainless.
The detailed explanation is that by those [means] through which you abandon all conceptual constructions along with their associations, you thereby attain the form of awakening; thus it is said:
"This is that Self, this is the Supreme, whom no one can fully comprehend."
"Even though the self is liberated, it is encircled by that very [bond] which was bound;

thus, even if one has been released from that bond by which the self was imagined and conceptualized as 'this is the self' and 'this is the other,' it has not then attained its true nature and is therefore not liberated.
Therefore, the distinction between self and other is not to be made. This is what is meant here.

"Do not entertain the delusion that the other and the self are two distinct things; rather, [realize] the entire realm of sentient beings as being from the very beginning uninterrupted and pure by its own nature, like a stainless supreme jewel. (146) Furthermore, do not create the delusion that the other and the self exist in a dual form; instead, [know that] from the very beginning, the entire realm of sentient beings is pure by its own nature. From that very beginning, through meditative cultivation, it is [revealed to be] veiled by infinite defilements.
The Buddhas do not cultivate a self.

Thus, by being free from duality, that Buddha is the stainless, supreme consciousness—the nature of form which is the *bodhicitta*—due to its lack of intrinsic nature: "O you who are the very essence of the mind, may you spread throughout the three worlds!"
"Compassion bears blossoms and fruit; know it to be the supreme relief.

When this was said, he indicated the benefit to others: "May the King of Existence (Bhavārāja) uphold that non-dual mind of yogis, which, like a wish-fulfilling tree, pervades the entire expanse of the three worlds."
The intended meaning is that everything is supreme non-duality (*paramādvaya*).
Through the blossoming of the flower of his compassion, that [non-duality] becomes fully blossomed;
it is not by this that he performs benefit for others.

Because it brings to fulfillment the purity and other qualities of all [beings] and all [perfections], they [are characterized] by that. The tree of emptiness has blossomed with various kinds of compassion;
another fruit is the enjoyment of others—this is the supreme bliss in the mind.

Where the excellent trees are empty and pitiless, having neither root nor trunk, he who provides support at their base receives a share of their burden. For that reason, each tree bears but a single fruit.
And he who knows this distinction is liberated from both existence and nirvana.
(147) He who remains established in the state of non-existence, if he goes forth free from desire, let him cast off this household life like a beggar discarding a broken earthenware bowl.

"May he fall!"—thus, having abandoned that thought in their minds, those who possess compassion for sentient beings [reflect]: "From whom does this come? If anyone who is a petitioner goes away disappointed, thinking 'nothing was given to me by this person or by the world'..."
At that time, whatever may be accomplished occurs;
therefore, you wander for alms with a broken bowl and are not attached to enjoyments.
You are abandoning this excellent household life—
as it has been said:
"No service was performed for others, nor was any gift bestowed."
"What fruit is there in this saṃsāra? Abandon yourself!
Thus [it is said]. What is accomplished by that enjoyment or by that house, since no benefit to others occurs?
There is wealth and the like, yet it is not given as a gift.
And what fruit does this wealth bring while one remains thus in saṃsāra? It brings nothing; rather, it is better that we abandon this very self.
Thinking, "I shall not dwell with indifference toward body and life," [ends] this commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Dihākoṣa*.
Regarding the phrase "of one whose speech has fallen away":
by that, this reality (tattva) was both obscured and revealed;
it was made a source of wonder among the ignorant folk.
And having composed this *pañjikā* for him, titled *Ātmabodhinī*,
it is also called *Ātmavedhinī*, which illuminates the oral tradition of the Guru.
And having looked upon others, perform even the [meditation on] the dharmas;
since whatever merit has been accomplished by me, whether for my own sake or for the sake of others,
by that merit may the world become the ground of knowledge of the Self-Existent One.
This commentary on the *Dohākoṣa* is completed.
Its extent is eight hundred [verses]. This work is by the venerable Advayavajra.
